API-001.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite, Postman, or curl) capable of precise request timing, and a scripting environment (Python) to send repeated requests and statistically analyze response-time distributions. A list of candidate usernames/emails to test (a mix of known-valid and known-invalid values, where available).
API-001.whatItIs: An endpoint like login, password reset, or account lookup takes noticeably longer to respond when the submitted username or email actually belongs to a real account, versus when it doesn't. That happens because checking a real account (looking it up, then comparing a password) does more work than instantly failing on one that doesn't exist. That timing gap is consistent enough that an attacker can use it to figure out which usernames or emails are real, just by measuring response times.
API-001.rootCause: The code takes a shortcut and stops immediately when a lookup fails, instead of always doing the same amount of work whether the account exists or not. That shortcut seems reasonable on its own — why compare a password against an account that isn't even there — but it accidentally creates a measurable difference in response time that reveals whether an account exists, before a password is ever actually checked.
API-001.impact: An attacker can quietly confirm which usernames and email addresses are real, at scale, without tripping any account lockout. Depending on the endpoint, no real login attempt is needed — only a lookup. That confirmed list then feeds everything else: more convincing phishing, credential stuffing aimed only at accounts known to exist, and password-reset abuse against real users.
stepsToIdentify: Send repeated requests to the target endpoint (login, password-reset, or registration-check) with a mix of known-valid and known-invalid usernames/emails, precisely measuring response time for each.

Send a sufficiently large sample (dozens to hundreds of requests per category) to smooth out network jitter, and compute the average and distribution of response times for the valid-account group versus the invalid-account group.
Confirm the timing difference is statistically significant and consistent across multiple test runs, rather than a one-off network artifact.
Where a difference is confirmed, test against a set of unknown-status usernames to demonstrate the technique successfully classifies them as valid or invalid based purely on timing.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes timing-based enumeration testing against the target endpoint.
Establish a timing baseline using a small set of known-valid and known-invalid accounts (test accounts provided by the client).
Automate submission of a larger candidate list (from OSINT, a common-username wordlist, or client-provided scope) while recording precise response times for each.

Classify each candidate as likely-valid or likely-invalid based on which timing distribution its response falls into, cross-checking a sample against ground truth where available to calculate the technique's accuracy.
Document the confirmed timing differential (in milliseconds), the classification accuracy achieved, and the specific endpoint(s) affected.

examplePayloads.label: Measure response time for a batch of candidate usernames
examplePayloads.command:
python3 -c "
import requests, time
for user in open('candidates.txt'):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    requests.post('https://api.target.com/login', json={'username': user.strip(), 'password': 'wrong'})
    print(user.strip(), time.perf_counter() - t0)
"

examplePayloads.label: Statistically compare timing distributions for known-valid vs known-invalid accounts

variants: Timing side-channel on a password-reset endpoint (revealing account existence via a different processing path for sending vs. not sending a reset email) rather than the login endpoint specifically.
Timing difference introduced not by the lookup itself but by a downstream action only performed for valid accounts (e.g. an async email-send call that adds measurable latency to the response).
mitigation: Ensure the endpoint performs a constant amount of work regardless of whether the account exists — always perform a (dummy, fixed-cost) hash comparison even when the lookup fails, so the total processing time doesn't depend on account existence.
Return an identical, generic response message and status code for both valid and invalid account scenarios, removing any content-based enumeration vector alongside the timing one.

Where the endpoint's slow path involves an unavoidable async action (sending an email), decouple that action from the response entirely (return immediately, process the send in the background) so its latency doesn't leak into the response timing.
Apply consistent rate limiting to the endpoint regardless of this fix, since it provides defense in depth against enumeration attempts generally.

API-002.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite, Postman) and a content-discovery/fuzzing tool (ffuf, gobuster) with a wordlist targeting common debug/admin/actuator endpoint paths.
API-002.whatItIs: The live, public API exposes debug or admin endpoints that were only ever meant for internal or development use. Common examples are an auto-generated debug console, a diagnostic endpoint dumping configuration and environment details, GraphQL's introspection feature, or an API documentation page revealing the entire internal API surface. All of them are reachable by anyone who knows or guesses the URL, with no extra login required.
API-002.rootCause: A lot of frameworks turn these debug tools on by default while you're developing, for convenience. Turning them off (or locking them behind an internal-only network or extra login) before going live is a separate step that's easy to forget, and nothing in the release process automatically checks for it.
API-002.impact: How serious this is depends entirely on which endpoint is exposed. At the lower end it leaks information — internal configuration, environment variables, dependency versions, or a full schema that maps the whole API for an attacker. At the upper end it hands over administrative functionality with no login at all, such as a debug console that runs arbitrary code or an endpoint that changes configuration. The specific endpoint decides whether this is a minor leak or critical.
stepsToIdentify: Run a content-discovery/fuzzing scan against the target API's base path using a wordlist targeting common debug/admin/actuator/introspection endpoint names for the apparent backend framework (Spring Boot Actuator paths, Django debug toolbar, GraphQL `/graphql` with introspection enabled).
For any discovered candidate, confirm it's reachable without authentication (or with only the same authentication level as an ordinary, low-privilege API consumer).
Where a GraphQL endpoint is found, attempt an introspection query directly to check whether the full schema (including any undocumented or sensitive fields/mutations) is exposed.
Where a Swagger/OpenAPI spec endpoint is found, review its contents for any documented internal-only or deprecated-but-still-functional endpoints not intended for the public API surface.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes content-discovery scanning and interaction with any discovered debug/admin endpoints.
Run the fuzzing scan and confirm which candidate debug/admin/introspection endpoints are reachable without proper authentication.
For each reachable endpoint, document what information or functionality it exposes (configuration dump, environment variables, full schema, administrative actions).
Where the endpoint exposes genuinely sensitive configuration (database connection strings, internal service URLs, credentials), flag this as the primary impact evidence.
Where the endpoint exposes administrative functionality, demonstrate a benign, non-destructive action (if authorized) to confirm real exploitability rather than just informational exposure.

examplePayloads.label: Fuzz for common debug/admin/actuator endpoint paths
Test for exposed Spring Boot Actuator endpoints specifically
Attempt a GraphQL introspection query
examplePayloads.command: curl -s -X POST https://api.target.com/graphql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":"{__schema{types{name fields{name}}}}"}' | jq .

variants: GraphQL introspection left enabled in production, exposing the complete schema (including undocumented mutations/fields) to any caller, versus a REST-specific debug endpoint dumping configuration.
Swagger/OpenAPI documentation endpoint exposed publicly and listing genuinely internal-only endpoints not intended for external consumers, distinct from a framework debug console.
mitigation: Disable all debug/diagnostic endpoints and consoles in production builds, verified via an automated release-gate check rather than manual configuration review alone.
Disable GraphQL introspection in production, or restrict it to authenticated, internal-only callers if it must remain available for tooling purposes.

Restrict any genuinely necessary actuator/health-check endpoint to an internal-only network path or a separate, strongly-authenticated management port, never on the same publicly-reachable listener as the primary API.
Restrict Swagger/OpenAPI documentation endpoints to authenticated access, or ensure the published spec only documents the intended, public-facing API surface.

API-003.prerequisites: A browser or an API client capable of sending a custom `Origin` header (curl, Burp Suite). Knowledge or discovery of the internal microservice's API base URL, reachable from a browser context (e.g. via the corporate network, a VPN, or because the service is inadvertently internet-facing).
API-003.whatItIs: An internal service — not meant to be called directly from a browser at all — has a setting that automatically trusts whatever website is asking (reflecting back whatever 'origin' the request claims to be from), often combined with allowing credentials to be sent along too. That means a malicious webpage, loaded in the browser of someone who happens to have network access to that internal service (say, through a VPN), can make an authenticated request to it and read the response.
API-003.rootCause: This setting was configured too permissively — automatically trusting any requesting website instead of a specific, known list — likely because the developers never expected this internal service to be reachable from a random browser at all. They didn't account for the fact that anyone with network access to the service, including a victim's browser over VPN, effectively extends the boundary of who can reach it.
API-003.impact: A malicious web page can make authenticated requests to the internal API using the victim's own session, then read the responses. The victim only needs to be able to reach that service — on the corporate VPN, on the internal network, or where the service is unintentionally internet-facing. The attacker can pull internal data or perform state-changing actions the victim is authorised for, and the victim never notices.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the internal microservice's API endpoints reachable from a browser context (via the tester's own VPN/network access, with authorization).

Send a request to the API with a crafted, arbitrary `Origin` header (e.g. `https://evil-test.example.com`) and inspect whether the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header reflects that same arbitrary origin back.

Check whether `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` is also present alongside the reflected origin, which is the combination that enables a malicious page to actually read authenticated response data (browsers require this pairing for credentialed cross-origin reads to succeed).
Confirm the API endpoint being tested actually returns or acts on sensitive, authenticated data, since CORS misconfiguration on a genuinely public, non-sensitive endpoint carries much lower impact.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes CORS-misconfiguration testing against the target internal microservice API.
Send a test request with an arbitrary `Origin` header and confirm the reflected-origin/credentials-allowed response pattern.
Build a benign proof-of-concept HTML page that issues a credentialed `fetch()`/XHR request to the internal API from a different origin, hosted on a test domain.

Load the proof-of-concept page in a browser session authenticated to the internal service (a test account) and confirm the cross-origin response is successfully read by the malicious page's JavaScript.
Document the exact reflected-origin behavior, the sensitive data/action exposed, and the browser-reachability precondition (VPN/internal network) required for real-world exploitation.

examplePayloads.label: Test for origin reflection in the CORS policy
Proof-of-concept cross-origin credentialed request page

variants: CORS misconfiguration on an internal API that's also inadvertently internet-facing, removing the VPN/internal-network precondition entirely and making it exploitable from any internet-connected victim.

Origin validation that checks only a substring/suffix of the Origin header (e.g. accepting anything ending in `.target.com`), bypassable by registering a subdomain-lookalike or using a crafted origin that satisfies the substring check.
mitigation: Configure CORS with an explicit allowlist of specific, trusted origins rather than reflecting the request's Origin header dynamically.
Never combine a wildcard or reflected-origin CORS policy with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.

For internal-only microservices, prefer restricting network reachability (so the service genuinely isn't reachable from a browser context at all) over relying on CORS as the primary access-control mechanism.
Periodically re-test CORS configuration after any framework/library update, since default CORS-handling behavior sometimes changes between versions.

API-004.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman) and a JWT-manipulation tool (jwt_tool, or Burp's JWT Editor extension). A valid JWT issued to a test account for the target API.
API-004.whatItIs: The API's login-token system (JWT) has a weakness that lets someone forge or tamper with a token and have it accepted as real. This might mean the server accepts a token that says 'no signature needed' and skips checking it entirely, accepts a token that was supposed to be signed one way but got re-signed a different, weaker way using a key that's actually meant to be public, or uses a weak, guessable secret that can be cracked offline.
API-004.rootCause: Many JWT systems let the token itself specify which method should be used to verify it. If the server just trusts whatever the token claims instead of insisting on one specific, expected method, an attacker can manipulate that field to trick the server into either skipping verification entirely, or checking the signature against the wrong kind of key.
API-004.impact: An attacker who can forge a token the server accepts can impersonate any user, including an administrator, by simply setting the identity they want in the token. That is a complete authentication bypass along with whatever the forged claims authorise. It ranks among the most severe API findings possible, because it defeats the entire authentication scheme in a single step rather than working around it.
stepsToIdentify: Decode a captured, valid JWT (base64-decode the header and payload) and inspect the `alg` field and claim structure.
Attempt to modify the token to use `alg: none` (removing the signature entirely) and resubmit it to a protected endpoint, checking whether the server accepts it.

If the server uses RS256, attempt the algorithm-confusion attack: re-sign the token using HS256 with the server's publicly-available RSA public key (often exposed via a JWKS endpoint or embedded in client-side code) as the HMAC secret.
If neither of the above succeeds, attempt to brute-force the HMAC secret offline against a captured HS256 token using a wordlist of common/weak secrets.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes JWT forgery/tampering testing against the target API.
Capture a valid JWT for a test account and decode its structure.
Attempt the `alg: none` bypass by modifying the header and stripping the signature, then submit the modified token to a protected endpoint.
If unsuccessful, attempt the RS256-to-HS256 algorithm-confusion attack using the server's public key as the HMAC secret.
If a forged token is accepted, modify the payload's claims (user ID, role) to impersonate a higher-privileged user and confirm the resulting elevated access.
Document the exact bypass technique that succeeded and the resulting impersonation achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Automated JWT vulnerability scanning with jwt_tool
Manually craft an alg:none forged token
examplePayloads.command:
python3 -c "
import base64, json
header = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps({'alg':'none','typ':'JWT'}).encode()).rstrip(b'=')
payload = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps({'sub':'admin','role':'admin'}).encode()).rstrip(b'=')
print((header + b'.' + payload + b'.').decode())
"

examplePayloads.label: RS256-to-HS256 algorithm confusion using the server's public key as HMAC secret

variants: Weak/guessable HMAC secret brute-forceable offline via a wordlist (jwt_tool/hashcat mode 16500), rather than an algorithm-confusion or none-algorithm bypass.

JWT signature correctly verified, but the token's expiration (`exp`) claim not actually enforced server-side, allowing indefinite reuse of an old, expired token (overlapping with the improper-session-handling class of finding).
mitigation: Enforce a single, explicitly-expected signing algorithm server-side, rejecting any token whose header specifies a different algorithm rather than trusting the header's stated algorithm.
Never accept `alg: none` under any circumstance in production.
Use a strong, sufficiently random HMAC secret (or, preferably, asymmetric signing with a properly-protected private key) and rotate it if any compromise is suspected.
Validate all standard JWT claims (`exp`, `iat`, `aud`, `iss`) server-side on every request, not just the signature.

API-005.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman), and a content-discovery/fuzzing tool for broader configuration-surface enumeration. Access to the API's documented endpoints as a starting point for a systematic configuration review.
API-005.whatItIs: The API has a collection of smaller security-configuration issues that don't fit neatly into one specific category on their own — overly detailed error messages that leak internal file paths, missing standard security headers, sample or default endpoints still switched on, or settings that differ between the test and production environments. Together, they suggest the API wasn't run through a standard hardening checklist before it went live.
API-005.rootCause: Security configuration is made up of a lot of small settings — error message detail, security headers, removing default content — and none of them has one obvious owner or one single check that catches all of them together. Without a systematic hardening review before release, these small gaps just accumulate.
API-005.impact: Taken one at a time these are usually minor — a verbose error helping reconnaissance, a missing header slightly weakening browser protections. Their significance is cumulative: together they lower the bar for an attacker mapping and probing the API. Occasionally one escalates on its own, as when a stack trace reveals a library version with a known critical vulnerability.
stepsToIdentify: Trigger a variety of error conditions against the API (malformed input, missing required fields, an internal server error) and review whether the response leaks a stack trace, internal file paths, or library/framework version details.

Review HTTP response headers across representative endpoints for standard security headers (`Strict-Transport-Security`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Content-Security-Policy` where applicable to any API-served HTML/documentation).
Check for default/sample content (a framework's default welcome page, an example endpoint) left enabled at the API's base path.
Where multiple environments (staging, production) are accessible for comparison, check whether production has drifted from an intended, more hardened baseline configuration.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes triggering error conditions and reviewing configuration across the target API.
Systematically trigger a range of error conditions and document any verbose error content leaked in each response.
Review response headers across a representative sample of endpoints and note any missing standard security headers.
Where a leaked stack trace/version detail reveals a specific library version, cross-reference it against known CVEs for that version as a potential escalation path.
Compile the full list of individual misconfigurations found as a consolidated finding, since a checklist-style hardening remediation addresses many of them at once.

examplePayloads.label: Trigger a malformed-input error to check for verbose stack-trace leakage
Review security response headers across the API
Check for default/sample content at the API base path

variants: Verbose error messages present only on unhandled/500-level errors versus present even on ordinary, expected 400-level validation errors.
Security headers missing consistently across the entire API versus present on some endpoints but not others due to inconsistent middleware application.
mitigation: Configure a global error handler that returns a generic, non-verbose error message and status code in production, logging the full detail server-side only.
Apply standard security response headers consistently across all API responses via a single, centrally-applied middleware rather than per-endpoint configuration.
Remove all default/sample/example content from the production deployment.
Adopt a documented, checklist-driven security-hardening standard applied consistently across every environment, and periodically re-audit for configuration drift between environments.

API-006.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman). Access to the API's authentication endpoints and, ideally, a test account for baseline comparison against any bypass attempt.
API-006.whatItIs: There's a real gap in how the API checks who you are — an endpoint that should require login but doesn't, a login check that can be satisfied with an empty or malformed value, or a password-reset process that can be completed without actually proving you own the account being reset.
API-006.rootCause: Either the login requirement was simply left off a specific endpoint — often one added later that didn't follow the same standard pattern used elsewhere in the API — or the login-checking logic itself has a flaw that a specifically crafted, invalid input can slip through without a real, valid credential.
API-006.impact: An attacker reaches protected data or functionality without ever holding valid credentials. This sits among the most severe API findings because it breaks the trust boundary every other authorisation check is built on top of. Once authentication can be skipped, the rest of the access control model has nothing to stand on.
stepsToIdentify: Systematically test every documented API endpoint by sending a request with no authentication token/credential at all, and separately with a malformed/empty one, checking whether any endpoint responds successfully rather than with a 401.

Review the API's password-reset/account-recovery flow specifically for whether it can be completed without proving ownership of the target account (e.g. a reset link/code that isn't properly validated, or a flow that reveals the reset token in a response rather than only sending it out-of-band).
Check for inconsistent authentication enforcement across similar endpoints (a v1 endpoint requiring auth, a v2 or newly-added equivalent endpoint that doesn't).

Where the API uses a gateway/middleware pattern for authentication, check whether every route is actually registered under that middleware, since a misconfigured route-registration order can leave specific endpoints unprotected.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes authentication-bypass testing against the target API.
Systematically request every documented endpoint without authentication and record which ones unexpectedly succeed.
For any endpoint found unprotected, confirm the actual data/functionality exposed.
If a password-reset flow flaw is identified, attempt to complete an account takeover for a nominated test account using the identified bypass, without needing the account's original credentials.
Document the exact unprotected endpoint(s) or authentication-flow flaw and the resulting unauthorized access achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Test an endpoint with no authentication header at all
Test with a malformed/empty Authorization header
Test a password-reset flow for ownership-verification gaps

variants: A newly-added endpoint simply omitted from the authentication middleware's route registration, versus a deliberate but flawed custom-authentication implementation on a specific endpoint.

Password-reset flow that reveals the reset token/code directly in an API response (rather than only sending it out-of-band via email/SMS), allowing an attacker to complete the reset without ever receiving the out-of-band message.
mitigation: Apply authentication middleware consistently and centrally across every route, verified via an automated test that confirms every endpoint requires authentication unless explicitly and deliberately marked public.
Never reveal a password-reset token/code in an API response; always deliver it exclusively via the intended out-of-band channel (email/SMS).
Include an authentication-bypass regression test suite covering every endpoint as part of routine CI/CD testing, not just periodic external assessments.
Review new endpoints specifically for correct authentication-middleware application as part of the code-review process before merge.

API-007.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman). Understanding of the API gateway's architecture — specifically whether it validates JWTs itself before forwarding to backend microservices, or merely passes the token through unchanged. A valid JWT for a test account, and a JWT-manipulation tool (jwt_tool) to craft tampered variants.
API-007.whatItIs: An API gateway sits in front of backend services and is supposed to check every login token before passing requests along. But a specific backend service — either reachable directly, bypassing the gateway, or reached through the gateway with a tampered token the gateway doesn't fully check — just trusts what the token claims without verifying it again itself. If the gateway's check can be skipped or fooled, the backend accepts forged information without question.
API-007.rootCause: It's a common but risky design to put all the login-checking responsibility at the gateway, and have every backend service just trust that anything reaching it has already been checked. But if the backend is also reachable directly, or if the gateway only does a shallow check (like just looking at the token's format, not its actual signature), that assumption — 'the gateway already handled this' — becomes a single point of failure instead of a real second layer of defense.
API-007.impact: An attacker who reaches the backend service directly, bypassing the gateway, or who crafts a token that satisfies whatever limited checking the gateway does, can present forged claims straight to the backend. The backend accepts them. The outcome is a full authentication bypass and impersonation, exactly as if that service had no authentication in front of it at all.
stepsToIdentify: Map the API gateway's architecture to identify backend microservice hostnames/IPs, checking whether any are directly reachable from outside the intended gateway-only network path (via DNS enumeration, an exposed internal load balancer, or a misconfigured network ACL).
Where a backend service is directly reachable, send a request with a forged/tampered JWT directly to it and observe whether it's accepted without independent signature verification.

Where the backend isn't directly reachable, test whether the gateway itself performs full signature verification versus only checking token structure/expiration, by sending a token with a tampered signature through the gateway and observing whether it's rejected at the gateway or passed through to the backend.

Cross-reference this finding with the general JWT-misconfiguration finding, since a gateway-passthrough issue is often compounded by a weak signature-verification implementation at whichever layer does perform it.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes both direct-backend-reachability testing and gateway-passthrough testing against the target API.
Attempt to identify and directly reach a backend microservice, bypassing the gateway.
If reachable, send a forged JWT with elevated-privilege claims directly to the backend and confirm whether it's accepted.
If the backend isn't directly reachable, test whether the gateway performs full signature verification, or merely token-structure validation, by passing a tampered-signature token through it.
Document the exact architectural gap (direct backend reachability, or insufficient gateway-level verification passed through to a trusting backend) and the resulting impersonation achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate potential direct backend hostnames
Send a forged JWT directly to a discovered backend service, bypassing the gateway
Test whether the gateway performs full signature verification

variants: Backend microservice directly reachable due to a network-boundary misconfiguration, versus the gateway itself performing insufficient validation that's passed through even via the intended gateway path.

Gateway validates the token's signature correctly but doesn't re-check claims (role, scope) on every subsequent hop, allowing a backend service further downstream to trust stale or overly broad claims from an otherwise validly-signed token.
mitigation: Ensure every backend microservice independently verifies the JWT's signature and claims, never relying solely on the assumption that the gateway already did so — defense in depth at each layer.
Restrict network reachability so backend microservices are genuinely unreachable except through the gateway (a properly enforced internal network boundary/service mesh policy).
Ensure the gateway itself performs full, correct signature verification (not just structural/expiration checks) before forwarding any request.
Periodically test for direct backend reachability as part of routine API security assessments, since network-boundary misconfigurations are a common and easy-to-overlook regression.

API-008.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite with Intruder, or a custom script) capable of sending a high volume of authentication requests. A list of candidate credentials (a small, representative wordlist for a bounded, authorized test) and a test account for establishing the baseline lockout threshold.
API-008.whatItIs: The login endpoint (or a related one, like OTP verification or password reset) accepts an unlimited number of attempts, with no slowdown, delay, or lockout after repeated failures. That lets an attacker try as many usernames and passwords as their network connection allows, as fast as it allows.
API-008.rootCause: Limiting login attempts takes deliberate extra work — tracking how many times someone's tried, per account or per IP, and enforcing a cutoff. That's easy to skip if the initial focus during development was just getting the normal login flow working, without a specific requirement to protect it against abuse.
API-008.impact: An attacker can run credential stuffing at high speed, testing large lists of username and password pairs leaked from other breaches, or brute-force a specific account. Given how common password reuse is, that has a realistic chance of working. With no lockout in place there is no friction and no alert, so the attempt can continue indefinitely.
stepsToIdentify: Send a bounded burst of authentication requests (with a nominated test account, using intentionally incorrect credentials) and observe whether any rate-limiting response (429) or account-lockout behavior engages after a defined number of failures.
If no lockout engages within a reasonable test volume, calculate the sustainable request rate against the endpoint to characterize the realistic brute-force feasibility.

Check whether rate limiting, if present, is keyed on a robust attribute (account identifier) versus an easily-rotated one (source IP alone), cross-referencing with the general rate-limit-bypass finding for that specific nuance.

Test the same absence-of-limiting condition against related endpoints (OTP verification, password-reset confirmation) which are equally valuable brute-force targets but sometimes overlooked if only the primary login endpoint was reviewed.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes a bounded, authorized brute-force/credential-stuffing simulation against a nominated test account.
Send an escalating burst of incorrect-credential attempts against the test account and confirm no lockout/rate-limiting engages within an agreed volume.
Where authorized and within a safe, bounded scope, run a representative-sized wordlist against the test account to demonstrate practical brute-force feasibility within a reasonable time budget.
Repeat the same absence-of-limiting test against OTP-verification and password-reset-confirmation endpoints specifically.
Document the confirmed absence of rate limiting/lockout, the sustainable attack rate achieved, and which specific endpoints are affected.

examplePayloads.label: Bounded burst of failed login attempts to test for lockout
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 50); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST https://api.target.com/login -d '{"username":"test-account","password":"wrong'$i'"}'; done

examplePayloads.label: Burp Intruder sniper attack against the login endpoint with a bounded wordlist
examplePayloads.command: # Burp Intruder: load captured login request, payload position on password field, use a representative bounded wordlist, monitor response codes for lockout onset

examplePayloads.label: Test OTP-endpoint brute-force feasibility given a small code space
examplePayloads.command: for otp in $(seq -w 0000 0100); do curl -s -X POST https://api.target.com/otp/verify -d '{"code":"'$otp'"}'; done

variants: No rate limiting on the primary login endpoint specifically, versus login correctly rate-limited but an adjacent, equally sensitive endpoint (OTP verification, password-reset confirmation) left unprotected.
Rate limiting present but keyed on source IP only, bypassable via IP rotation (overlaps with the rate-limit-bypass finding).
mitigation: Implement progressive rate limiting/lockout on every authentication-related endpoint (login, OTP verification, password-reset confirmation), keyed on account identifier in addition to source IP.
Apply CAPTCHA or an equivalent proof-of-work challenge after a small number of failed attempts to further slow automated abuse.
Alert on abnormal authentication-failure volume patterns as a detective control complementing the preventive rate limit.
Ensure verification codes (OTP) have sufficient entropy and a short expiry window so that even a moderate rate limit makes brute-force impractical within the code's validity period.

API-009.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman) and valid credentials/tokens for at least two accounts of different privilege levels (a standard user and an administrator, if the API has role distinctions).
API-009.whatItIs: The API checks that you're logged in, but doesn't check that your account actually has permission to do the specific thing you're asking for. So a regular user can successfully call an endpoint, or trigger an action, that should really be restricted to admins only — just because the check stops at 'are you logged in' instead of 'are you allowed to do this specific thing.'
API-009.rootCause: Checking who someone is (are they logged in) and checking what they're allowed to do (do they have the right role for this specific action) are two different checks — and it's common for an endpoint to correctly do the first while skipping or only partly doing the second. This especially happens with admin-only endpoints added later that don't consistently reuse the same permission check used elsewhere.
API-009.impact: An ordinary low-privilege user can call administrative functions directly — creating or deleting other people's accounts, changing system-wide configuration, or reaching an admin-only reporting endpoint. How far that goes depends on which functions are affected. It ranges from a significant data exposure to complete administrative control of the application.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate the API's documented (and, via content discovery, undocumented) endpoints and identify which are intended to be restricted to a specific, elevated role based on naming conventions, documentation, or observed UI-level access restrictions.
Using a low-privilege test account's valid token, attempt to call each identified admin/elevated-role endpoint directly.
Confirm whether the endpoint correctly rejects the low-privilege caller (403) or unexpectedly processes the request.
Where an endpoint is found vulnerable, confirm the actual functional impact by observing what the low-privilege account was able to achieve (data returned, a state change made).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes function-level authorization testing using accounts of differing privilege levels.
Capture a legitimate administrator's request to a privilege-restricted endpoint (with authorization, using a test admin account) to understand the expected request structure.
Replay the same request structure using a low-privilege test account's authentication token instead.
Confirm whether the low-privilege account's request is processed successfully rather than being rejected.
Document the exact endpoint, the privilege-check gap, and the resulting unauthorized functionality/data access achieved.

examplePayloads.command: # Burp: capture the request an admin test account makes to an admin-only endpoint, e.g. POST /admin/users/delete

Systematically test a list of suspected admin endpoints with a low-privilege token

variants: A REST endpoint missing a function-level role check entirely, versus a GraphQL mutation reachable by any authenticated user despite being intended as admin-only, since GraphQL's single-endpoint model makes it easier to overlook per-mutation authorization checks.
The API's own UI correctly hides the restricted functionality from low-privilege users (so the vulnerability is invisible through normal use) while the underlying endpoint remains callable directly.
mitigation: Implement and consistently apply a function-level authorization check (a role/permission decorator or middleware) on every endpoint, verified via an automated test suite asserting the expected role requirement for each.
Never rely on UI-level hiding of restricted functionality as a substitute for server-side authorization enforcement.

Apply the principle of least privilege by default — require an explicit, positive role/permission grant for access rather than defaulting to allow-all and only restricting specific known-sensitive endpoints.
Include function-level authorization test cases (attempting every endpoint with each defined role) in routine regression testing, not just periodic external assessments.

API-010.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman) and valid credentials/tokens for at least two separate, equally-privileged test accounts (to demonstrate one account accessing another's data).
API-010.whatItIs: An endpoint that takes an ID — a user ID, an order ID, a document ID — in the request returns or changes that specific item without checking that the person asking actually owns it or is allowed to access it. A logged-in user can simply swap in someone else's ID, and the endpoint will process it as if it were their own.
API-010.rootCause: The endpoint correctly checks that you're logged in, but the check stops there — it never goes on to verify the specific item you're asking about actually belongs to you. The database query or update is filtered only by the ID you supplied, with no extra condition tying it back to your own account.
API-010.impact: Any logged-in user can read or change any other user's data by swapping one identifier in an otherwise normal API call. This is consistently the most common and most damaging API vulnerability class found in real assessments. The reason is scale: it is trivially automatable, so it exposes data across every account the API serves rather than one unlucky victim.
stepsToIdentify: Using test account A, perform a normal, legitimate API action that references an object ID belonging to account A (viewing an order, a profile, a document).
Using test account B's authentication token, replay the identical request but substitute account A's object ID in place of account B's own.
Confirm whether the response returns account A's data despite the request being authenticated as account B, or whether the API correctly rejects the mismatch.

Where object IDs are sequential/predictable (auto-incrementing integers), assess whether this also enables straightforward enumeration of every other user's objects, compounding the finding's severity.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cross-account object-access testing using the provided test accounts.
Capture a legitimate request from test account A referencing one of its own object IDs.
Replay the identical request using test account B's authentication token, with account A's object ID substituted in.
Confirm the response returns or modifies account A's data despite being authenticated as account B.

Where object IDs are sequential, demonstrate the broader impact by enumerating a small, bounded range of IDs to confirm mass accessibility across multiple accounts (using only test accounts, not real user data).
Document the exact endpoint, the missing ownership check, and the confirmed cross-account access achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Capture account A's legitimate request to its own object
Replay with account B's token against account A's object ID
Enumerate a bounded range of sequential object IDs to confirm mass accessibility (test accounts only)
examplePayloads.command: for id in $(seq 1000 1010); do curl -s https://api.target.com/orders/$id -H "Authorization: Bearer <account-B-token>"; done

variants: BOLA on a GraphQL resolver (querying a node by ID without ownership verification) rather than a REST path parameter specifically.
BOLA on a write/update/delete operation (modifying or deleting another user's object) rather than a read-only data-exposure case, which is materially more severe.
mitigation: Enforce object-level ownership verification on every endpoint that accepts an object identifier — scope every query/update/delete to the authenticated caller's own records (`WHERE owner_id = current_user_id`) rather than trusting the supplied ID alone.

Use non-sequential, non-guessable object identifiers (UUIDs) as a defense-in-depth measure, understanding this doesn't replace proper authorization checks but does remove trivial enumeration as a compounding factor.
Include object-level authorization test cases (attempting cross-account access with two test accounts) in routine regression testing for every endpoint accepting an object ID.

Apply a centralized authorization-check pattern/middleware consistently across the API rather than reimplementing ownership checks ad hoc per endpoint, reducing the chance of a missed check on a newly-added route.

API-011.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman) and a valid test account's authentication token. Access to the API's documented response schema (or the ability to inspect a full response) to identify all available object properties, including ones not shown in the primary application UI.
API-011.whatItIs: An endpoint correctly checks that you own the specific item you're accessing, but doesn't check which specific fields of that item you're allowed to see or change. You might be able to view sensitive fields the app's own screen never shows you but the API sends back anyway — or change a field, like an account balance or a permission flag, that the real app never lets you edit, simply because the API accepts and processes whatever fields you happen to include in your request.
API-011.rootCause: Checking that someone owns an item, and checking which specific parts of that item they're allowed to touch, are two separate checks. The second one is easy to skip if an endpoint just returns the entire underlying data record on reads, or accepts and applies the entire request body on writes, instead of explicitly listing exactly which fields are allowed for that specific user.
API-011.impact: On reads, the response exposes fields the caller was never meant to see — another user's private data carried inside a shared object, or internal system flags. On writes, the caller can change a field they should not control simply by including it in the request. That covers raising their own role, adjusting a financial balance, or altering an internal status, none of which the real interface ever offers as editable.
stepsToIdentify: Capture a full API response for an object the test account owns and compare it against what the application's UI actually displays, flagging any additional fields present in the raw response but not shown in the UI.

For any endpoint accepting a write/update request, capture the legitimate request body the UI sends, then attempt to add additional fields (a role, a status flag, a balance) not normally included and resubmit.
Confirm whether the additional field is silently accepted and applied, versus being ignored or rejected by the API.
Where a sensitive read-side field is exposed, confirm whether it varies per caller (indicating an intentional, if perhaps risky, design) or is a static value that shouldn't be shared at all.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes property-level authorization testing using a nominated test account.
Capture the full raw API response for a test object and identify any sensitive fields beyond what the UI displays.
Capture a legitimate update request and add an additional, normally-not-editable field (e.g. `"role":"admin"` or `"accountBalance":999999`) to the request body.
Resubmit the modified request and confirm whether the additional field is accepted and applied to the underlying object.
Document the exact endpoint, the specific over-exposed or over-writable field, and the resulting impact.

examplePayloads.label: Compare a full API response against what the UI displays
Attempt to inject an additional, normally-restricted field into an update request

variants: Excessive property exposure on read (a sensitive field returned but not displayed) versus excessive property authorization on write (an additional field silently accepted and applied) — the write variant overlaps significantly with the general mass-assignment finding.

The over-writable field is itself security-sensitive (a role/permission flag) versus merely a business-logic field (a discount percentage) — both are findings, but the former is typically far more severe.
mitigation: Explicitly allowlist the specific fields returned in every API response, based on the caller's role/context, rather than serializing the full underlying data model by default.
Explicitly allowlist the specific fields accepted and applied in every write/update request, ignoring or rejecting any field outside that allowlist rather than trusting the full request body.

Apply a consistent, centrally-defined schema/DTO (data transfer object) pattern for both requests and responses so field-level restrictions are enforced structurally rather than through ad hoc, per-endpoint logic.
Include property-level authorization test cases (attempting to read/write fields outside the intended, documented set) in routine regression testing.

API-012.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman). A valid test account's authentication token, and the ability to craft requests with missing, null, or otherwise malformed values for parameters the authorization logic depends on.
API-012.whatItIs: When a value the authorization check expects — like an owner ID or organization ID — is missing or blank in a specific situation, the check ends up accidentally passing instead of correctly failing. For example, a comparison like 'does the requested owner ID match my own owner ID' might evaluate as true simply because both sides are empty or missing, rather than being explicitly rejected as invalid.
API-012.rootCause: The authorization logic was written assuming its inputs would always be present and properly filled in, and the specific case of a missing or blank value was never explicitly tested. Depending on the programming language and how the comparison is written, two missing values can accidentally 'match' each other, silently turning what should be a hard failure into an unintended pass.
API-012.impact: An attacker who works out which parameter causes this — by omitting it or setting it to null — bypasses the authorisation check entirely for that code path. They never have to satisfy the condition the check was actually written to enforce. That can mean reaching another user's data or a restricted function outright.
stepsToIdentify: For each authorization-sensitive endpoint, systematically test variations where an authorization-relevant parameter is omitted entirely, set to `null`, set to an empty string, or set to a type-mismatched value (a string where a number is expected).

Compare the response for each variation against both the expected-success case (a legitimate value) and the expected-failure case (an explicitly wrong value) to identify any variation that unexpectedly behaves like the success case.
Where a specific null/missing-value variation succeeds unexpectedly, confirm the resulting data/functionality accessed to establish concrete impact rather than just an anomalous response code.
Prioritize testing this pattern on endpoints involving multi-tenant or ownership-scoped data specifically, since that's where the impact of a bypassed check is most severe.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes systematic edge-case parameter testing (null/missing/malformed values) against the target API's authorization-sensitive endpoints.
Capture a legitimate, successful request to an authorization-sensitive endpoint as the baseline.
Systematically vary the authorization-relevant parameter(s) to null, omitted, empty-string, and type-mismatched values, resubmitting each and recording the response.
For any variation that unexpectedly succeeds, confirm the actual data/functionality accessed as proof of the bypass.
Document the exact parameter, the specific null/missing-value condition that triggered the bypass, and the resulting unauthorized access achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Test with the ownership/tenant parameter omitted entirely
Test with the parameter explicitly set to null in a JSON body
Test with a type-mismatched value for a numeric ownership field

variants: Null-value bypass affecting an object-level ownership check (overlapping with BOLA impact) versus a function-level role check (overlapping with BFLA impact) — the underlying root cause is the same edge-case-handling gap, but the impact category differs.

The bypass condition triggers only with a specific data type/language runtime's coercion behavior (e.g. loose equality in JavaScript) rather than being a universal pattern across all backend implementations.
mitigation: Explicitly validate that every authorization-relevant parameter is present and well-formed before evaluating any comparison logic, treating a missing/null value as an immediate, hard authorization failure rather than allowing it to flow into a comparison at all.
Use strict equality/type-checking in authorization comparisons rather than relying on a language's loose-equality or type-coercion behavior.
Include edge-case (null/missing/malformed parameter) test cases specifically in the authorization-logic test suite, not just happy-path and explicitly-wrong-value cases.
Adopt a fail-closed design principle throughout the authorization layer — any unexpected or unhandled input condition should result in access denial, never an implicit allow.

API-013.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) and sqlmap for automated exploitation. A valid test account's authentication token if the vulnerable parameter sits behind an authenticated endpoint.
API-013.whatItIs: An endpoint builds a database (or similar) query by directly pasting a caller-supplied value into the query text, instead of using the safe, standard method (a parameterized query) that keeps user input clearly separated from the query's actual logic. This lets an attacker inject extra query syntax that changes what the query actually does — pulling out extra data, bypassing a login check, or in the worst cases, taking over the database or server entirely.
API-013.rootCause: The value from the request is treated as safe, well-formed text and pasted directly into the query instead of being passed in as pure data the query engine can never interpret as instructions. This distinction — safe parameterized queries versus risky string-pasting — is well known and usually done correctly, but a specific endpoint (often one added later, or using an older coding pattern) can still get it wrong.
API-013.impact: How far this goes depends on the injection point and the engine behind it. At minimum an attacker extracts arbitrary data from the database, sidestepping every access control the application enforces. It can also become an authentication bypass, by injecting logic that always evaluates true. On some database engines and configurations it reaches further still, into operating system command execution through the database's own built-in functionality.
stepsToIdentify: Identify every API parameter that plausibly feeds into a backend query — search/filter parameters, sort-order fields, ID lookups — as the priority candidates for testing.

Send a single quote or other syntax-breaking character as the parameter value and observe whether the response changes to a database error, a different response structure, or an unhandled exception, which indicates the input reached a query without proper sanitization.
Where a syntax-breaking response is observed, use sqlmap (or manual boolean/time-based injection techniques) to confirm and characterize the injection more precisely.

Where the endpoint is authenticated, ensure testing is performed using the test account's own token, since this both keeps testing properly scoped and can reveal privilege-escalation-relevant injection points (e.g. an injectable parameter in a role-filtering query).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes injection testing against the target API endpoint and parameter.
Send a syntax-breaking test value and confirm an anomalous response indicating the input reached an unsanitized query.
Run sqlmap against the identified parameter to confirm and characterize the injection technique (boolean-based, time-based, UNION-based) applicable to the specific database engine in use.
Where confirmed, extract a minimal, non-destructive proof-of-concept data sample (e.g. the database version string, or a single test-account record) rather than performing a bulk data dump.
Document the exact endpoint, parameter, injection technique, and the specific data/impact demonstrated.

examplePayloads.label: Test for a syntax-breaking response with a single quote
Automated confirmation and exploitation with sqlmap
Manual boolean-based blind confirmation
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s "https://api.target.com/search?query=test' AND '1'='1" -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>"
curl -s "https://api.target.com/search?query=test' AND '1'='2" -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>"

variants: NoSQL injection (MongoDB operator injection via a JSON body parameter, e.g. `{"$ne": null}`) rather than classic SQL injection, requiring a different testing/exploitation approach specific to the query language in use.
Second-order injection, where the malicious input is stored via one endpoint and only triggers the injection when later processed by a different endpoint's query.
mitigation: Use parameterized queries/prepared statements (or the equivalent safe-query-construction API for the specific database/interpreter in use) for every query incorporating caller-supplied input, with no exceptions for "trusted" internal parameters.
Apply strict, allowlist-based input validation on every parameter as a defense-in-depth layer in addition to parameterized queries.
Apply the principle of least privilege to the database account the API uses, limiting the blast radius of any injection that does occur.
Include automated static/dynamic security testing (SAST/DAST with injection-specific rules) in the CI/CD pipeline to catch this class of vulnerability before release.

API-014.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite). A GraphQL API with a file-upload-capable resolver (commonly implementing the `graphql-multipart-request-spec`), and a listener you control (a Burp Collaborator instance or a simple netcat/HTTP listener) to confirm out-of-band request delivery.
API-014.whatItIs: A GraphQL file-upload resolver also accepts a URL — so a client can say "don't take my file, go grab it from this link instead" for things like importing an avatar or generating a thumbnail. The resolver fetches that link server-side with no restriction on where it's allowed to point. Because GraphQL bundles this into a mutation rather than a plainly-named REST endpoint, this particular path is frequently missed by both scanners and reviewers, even in organizations that have already locked down the equivalent problem on their REST endpoints.
API-014.rootCause: The URL-fetching branch of this resolver was added to support remote file import, but never inherited the destination allowlist applied elsewhere. Two things make GraphQL specifically prone to this: resolvers are often written per-field by different developers with no shared outbound-request helper enforcing restrictions, and security review tends to focus on the single /graphql endpoint's authentication rather than auditing what each individual resolver does once a request gets past it.
API-014.impact: An attacker makes the server issue requests on their behalf, reaching internal admin panels and APIs that are not otherwise reachable from the internet. The same trick points at the cloud provider's metadata service, which can return the instance's own credentials. The server's network position and trust do the work, taking the attacker somewhere they could never reach directly.
stepsToIdentify: Identify GraphQL mutations related to file upload/import that also accept a URL parameter, via introspection (if enabled) or documentation/schema review.

Submit a mutation with the URL parameter pointing to a listener you control (a Burp Collaborator payload or a netcat listener) and confirm whether an inbound request is received, proving the server fetches the URL.

Where confirmed, submit the same mutation with the URL parameter pointing at an internal/link-local address (a private IP range, `169.254.169.254` for cloud metadata) and observe the response for any reflected content indicating successful internal access.
Assess whether any URL-scheme/destination restriction is applied at all (does `file://` or `gopher://` also succeed, which would indicate an even broader SSRF primitive).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes SSRF testing via the target GraphQL resolver, including probing internal/link-local address ranges.
Submit a test mutation with the URL parameter pointing at a Collaborator/controlled listener to confirm out-of-band request delivery.
Submit the mutation with the URL parameter pointing at the cloud metadata service address (or another internal target agreed with the client) and inspect the response for reflected internal content.
Where metadata-service access is confirmed, attempt to retrieve IAM role credentials via the standard metadata-service path and validate their scope with a minimal, read-only check.
Document the exact resolver, parameter, and the specific internal resource/metadata successfully reached.

examplePayloads.label: Confirm out-of-band request delivery via a Collaborator/controlled listener
Probe the cloud metadata service via the resolver's URL parameter
Test alternate URL schemes for a broader SSRF primitive

variants: SSRF via a thumbnail/preview-generation resolver fetching a remote image URL, rather than a direct file-import mutation.

Blind SSRF (no response content reflected back) confirmable only via out-of-band interaction, versus a resolver that reflects fetched content directly in its response, enabling full internal-content disclosure.
mitigation: Restrict the resolver's URL-fetching functionality to an explicit allowlist of permitted schemes and destination hosts, rejecting any URL outside that allowlist.

Block requests to internal/link-local/loopback address ranges (RFC 1918 private ranges, `169.254.169.254`, `localhost`) at the network egress level from the application server, as defense in depth beyond application-level allowlisting.

Where cloud metadata access is genuinely needed by the application itself, use the more restrictive Instance Metadata Service v2 (IMDSv2) with a hop-limit restriction to reduce SSRF-based credential-theft risk.
Apply the same SSRF-prevention review rigor to GraphQL resolvers as is applied to equivalent REST endpoint functionality, since this is a common, newer blind spot.

API-015.prerequisites: Access to the target's public repositories, client-side code (mobile app decompilation, JavaScript bundle inspection), and documentation/support forums where a key might have been inadvertently shared. Standard secret-scanning tooling (gitleaks, truffleHog).
API-015.whatItIs: An API key ends up exposed through careless handling. It might be committed to a public code repository, embedded in website JavaScript or a mobile app that anyone can extract it from, or shared in a public forum or support ticket. A related problem is issuing one single all-powerful key used everywhere, instead of separate narrowly-scoped keys for each purpose. The key may authenticate to the target's own API or to a third-party service it connects to.
API-015.rootCause: API keys often get treated more casually than regular user passwords — there's usually no automated scanning catching an accidentally-committed key, no system limiting what a given key is actually allowed to do, and no regular rotation schedule to limit the damage if a key does leak.
API-015.impact: Anyone who finds the exposed key can authenticate as the legitimate integration and use whatever that key allows. At minimum that is unauthorised usage billed to the organisation. Where the key is not tightly scoped to a narrow set of functions, it is full data access instead.
stepsToIdentify: Search public source-control repositories, package registries, and paste sites for the organization's API key patterns using a secret-scanning tool and targeted search queries.
Decompile the organization's mobile app or inspect its client-side JavaScript bundles for embedded API keys.
Where a key is found, determine its scope of access (read-only vs. read-write, which specific resources/endpoints it can reach) by making a minimal, authorized test call.
Check whether the key-issuance process supports scoping/permission restriction at all, or whether every issued key is inherently all-powerful regardless of intended use case.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes searching for and validating exposed API keys related to the target organization.
Run secret-scanning across public repositories and any client-side code/binaries obtained through normal, legitimate access (downloading the public app/website).
For each candidate key found, validate its live status and scope of access using a minimal, read-only test call.
Document every discovered key, its exposure source, and its validated scope of access.
Recommend immediate rotation for any confirmed live, exposed key as an urgent finding.

examplePayloads.label: Search public repositories for the organization's API key patterns
Extract API keys embedded in a public JavaScript bundle
Validate a discovered key's scope with a minimal, read-only call

variants: A single, universal API key used across every client integration (mobile app, website, partner integrations) rather than distinct, scoped keys per use case, multiplying the impact of any single exposure.
Key exposed in a public support forum/ticket where a developer pasted a full request (including the key) while troubleshooting an integration issue.
mitigation: Issue distinct, narrowly-scoped API keys per integration/use case rather than a single universal key, limiting the blast radius of any individual key's exposure.
Add automated secret-scanning to the CI/CD pipeline and to public-facing client code builds specifically, catching accidental key inclusion before release.
Implement key rotation as a routine practice, and immediately rotate any key confirmed to have been exposed through any channel.

Never embed API keys directly in client-side code (JavaScript, mobile app binaries) distributed to end users; proxy any necessary third-party API calls through the organization's own backend, which holds the actual key.

API-016.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) capable of sending manually-crafted multipart/form-data requests with a custom, malformed boundary string. A file-upload-capable API endpoint.
API-016.whatItIs: A file-upload endpoint reads a special marker (called a 'boundary') to figure out where one part of the uploaded data ends and the next begins, but doesn't carefully double-check that marker against what's actually in the request. A carefully crafted, mismatched boundary can trick the parser into misreading the request — smuggling in extra fields that other validation never sees, or overwhelming the server with a malformed structure it handles inefficiently.
API-016.rootCause: Parsing this kind of upload format correctly is more complicated than it looks, and easy to get subtly wrong. If the library handling it (or a custom implementation) doesn't strictly and consistently apply that boundary marker across the entire request, a mismatch between what the client claims the structure is and what it actually is can be used to sneak content past checks that trust the parser's interpretation.
API-016.impact: What this yields depends on the specific parser weakness. An attacker may smuggle an extra form field or file part past upload validation, defeating a file-type or field-count restriction. A deliberately malformed structure can also cause a denial of service by making parsing expensive. Combined with a parsing mismatch elsewhere in the request chain, it can escalate into something closer to request smuggling.
stepsToIdentify: Capture a legitimate multipart file-upload request to understand its normal structure and boundary usage.

Craft variations with a malformed or inconsistent boundary — one that doesn't exactly match the boundary parameter declared in the `Content-Type` header, or one using unusual characters/casing — and observe how the server responds.
Attempt to smuggle an additional form field/part using a crafted boundary discrepancy, checking whether validation logic that should reject an unexpected field is bypassed.
Test the endpoint's resilience to a deliberately complex/malformed boundary structure for denial-of-service potential (a very high number of parts, an extremely long boundary string).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes malformed multipart-request testing against the target file-upload endpoint.
Capture and understand the baseline legitimate multipart request structure.
Craft a request with a deliberately malformed/inconsistent boundary designed to smuggle an additional field past validation.
Submit the crafted request and confirm whether the smuggled field is processed despite validation logic that should have rejected it.
Document the exact boundary-malformation technique used and the resulting validation bypass or denial-of-service impact observed.

examplePayloads.label: Capture a baseline legitimate multipart upload request
Craft a request with an inconsistent/malformed boundary to attempt field smuggling
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s -X POST https://api.target.com/upload \
  -H 'Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryABC' \
  --data-binary $'------WebKitFormBoundaryABC
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"

test content
------WebKitFormBoundaryXYZ
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="role"

admin
------WebKitFormBoundaryABC--'

variants: Boundary confusion used to smuggle an additional field past field-count/allowlist validation, versus used purely to trigger a resource-intensive parsing denial-of-service.
Discrepancy between the boundary the API gateway/WAF uses to inspect the request and the boundary the backend application actually parses with, enabling a WAF-bypass-style smuggling attack.
mitigation: Use a well-maintained, security-reviewed multipart-parsing library rather than a custom implementation, and keep it current against known parser-differential advisories.

Validate the request body's actual structure strictly matches the declared boundary throughout, rejecting any request where a discrepancy is detected rather than attempting to parse through it permissively.
Apply field-count and field-name allowlist validation after parsing is fully and correctly complete, not as an assumption baked into the parsing step itself.
Apply resource limits (maximum parts, maximum boundary length, maximum total request size) to bound the impact of any parsing-related denial-of-service attempt.

API-017.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) and, if source/decompiled code access is available, the ability to identify the specific regular expression used in the target's input-validation middleware.
API-017.whatItIs: A piece of code that validates input — checking an email or URL format, for example — uses a pattern-matching rule (a regex) that has a specific flaw: for a carefully crafted piece of text, checking it against that pattern takes exponentially longer the longer the text gets, instead of just a little longer. A single, modest-sized malicious input can lock up the server's processing power for an extremely long time — a denial-of-service from just one request.
API-017.rootCause: Certain ways of writing pattern-matching rules — specifically ones with nested, overlapping repetition — can behave fine on most inputs but blow up exponentially on a specific, crafted one. This kind of bug is easy to introduce completely by accident when writing what looks like a perfectly reasonable validation pattern, without realizing it has this hidden flaw.
API-017.impact: One crafted request, often only a few hundred characters, can pin a server process at full CPU for seconds or minutes depending on the input length. A small number of those sent concurrently exhausts the available worker processes entirely. At that point legitimate users are denied service, and the attacker spent almost nothing to achieve it.
stepsToIdentify: Identify input-validation middleware applied broadly across the API (email/URL format checks are common candidates) and, where source/decompiled access is available, review the actual regex patterns used for nested-quantifier or ambiguous-alternation constructs known to cause catastrophic backtracking.

Where source isn't available, test black-box by submitting progressively longer, structured test strings designed to probe for backtracking behavior (e.g. a long run of a repeated character followed by a character that breaks the expected pattern) and measuring response time growth relative to input length.

Confirm the growth in response time is exponential (or at least clearly super-linear) rather than a simple, bounded processing-time increase, distinguishing a genuine ReDoS finding from ordinary, larger-input processing overhead.
Assess which specific endpoints apply the vulnerable validation middleware, since a shared, widely-applied validation library multiplies this finding's impact across many endpoints at once.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes ReDoS testing against the target API, with an agreed, bounded approach to avoid genuinely denying service to a shared/production environment.
Where source/decompiled access is available, identify the exact vulnerable regex pattern and construct a mathematically-derived worst-case input string for it.

Where black-box only, iteratively test progressively crafted input strings while carefully measuring server response time, escalating cautiously and stopping well before genuinely impacting availability.
Demonstrate the vulnerability with a single request that causes a measurable, clearly disproportionate processing delay, rather than sending a sustained flood.
Document the exact vulnerable pattern/endpoint, the crafted input structure, and the measured processing-time impact.

examplePayloads.label: Test a classic catastrophic-backtracking-prone input pattern (nested quantifier probe)
Escalate input length cautiously while measuring response time growth
examplePayloads.command: for n in 10 15 20 25 30; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$n chars: %{time_total}s\n" -X POST https://api.target.com/validate-email -d '{"email":"'$(python3 -c "print('a'*$n + '!')")'"}'; done

variants: ReDoS in an email/URL validation regex specifically, versus in a broader text-sanitization or search-query-parsing regex applied more widely across the API.

ReDoS reachable pre-authentication (on a public registration/contact-form endpoint) versus only reachable by an already-authenticated user, which affects the finding's real-world exploitability and severity.
mitigation: Rewrite vulnerable regex patterns to avoid nested/ambiguous quantifier constructs known to cause catastrophic backtracking, or use a regex-linting tool (safe-regex, or an equivalent static analyzer) to catch this class of pattern before deployment.
Apply a strict input-length limit before any regex validation runs, bounding the worst-case processing time regardless of the pattern's own complexity characteristics.
Use a regex engine/library with a guaranteed linear-time matching guarantee (e.g. RE2-based implementations) for any pattern processing untrusted, variable-length input.
Apply a request-processing timeout at the application or infrastructure level as a backstop, killing any single request that exceeds a reasonable processing-time budget.

API-018.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman). Knowledge of the API's supported version range (via documentation, the `Accept`/custom version header, or the URL path structure) including any older, deprecated-but-still-functional versions.
API-018.whatItIs: The API supports multiple versions at once for backward compatibility, but an older version is still fully working even though it has weaker security than the current one — maybe a bug that's since been fixed reappears in the old version, or a security feature like rate limiting was simply never added to it. A client — or an attacker — can deliberately request that older, weaker version even while everything else about the interaction is otherwise current.
API-018.rootCause: Keeping every supported version equally secure forever is a lot of ongoing work, so it's common for a fix or security improvement made in the current version to never get applied back to older versions kept around just for compatibility. Assuming 'no one really uses the old version anymore' doesn't stop an attacker from deliberately choosing it specifically because it's weaker.
API-018.impact: An attacker deliberately asks for the older API version by changing a version parameter, header or path segment. That sidesteps any security control that exists only in the current version. They can reintroduce a vulnerability that was already fixed, escape stronger rate limiting, or exploit weaker input validation. As long as the old version stays reachable, improvements made to the current one count for nothing.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate all API versions the target supports, including undocumented or deprecated ones (via documentation, version-negotiation header/parameter fuzzing, or URL-path version enumeration).

For each older version found still functional, compare its security-relevant behavior against the current version — authentication requirements, rate limiting, input validation strictness — for any endpoint present in both.

Where a discrepancy is found, confirm the older version is genuinely reachable and functional (not just documented as deprecated but actually returning an error), by sending a real, representative request.
Assess whether version selection is purely client-driven (an attacker can simply specify the older version in a header/path) or requires some additional, harder-to-satisfy condition.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes testing against older/deprecated API versions of the target.
Identify a security control present in the current API version but confirmed absent/weaker in an older, still-functional version.

Send a request explicitly targeting the older version, structured to demonstrate the security control's absence (e.g. bypassing rate limiting, exploiting weaker input validation, or reintroducing a previously-fixed vulnerability).
Confirm the older version processes the request successfully despite what would be blocked or handled more securely by the current version.
Document the exact version-selection mechanism, the specific security discrepancy identified, and the resulting bypass demonstrated.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate supported API versions via a version header/parameter
examplePayloads.command: for v in v1 v2 v3 2020-01-01 2022-06-01; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$v: %{http_code}\n" -H "Accept-Version: $v" https://api.target.com/users/me; done

examplePayloads.label: Compare rate-limiting behavior between the current and an older API version
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 50); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} ' -H 'Accept-Version: v1' https://api.target.com/login -d '{"user":"test","pass":"wrong"}'; done; echo

examplePayloads.label: Test whether a previously-fixed vulnerability is reintroduced on the older version
examplePayloads.command: curl -s "https://api.target.com/v1/search?query=test'" -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>"  # compare against the equivalent, patched v3 endpoint's behavior for the same payload
