variants: Version selection via a simple, client-controlled header/parameter versus via the URL path itself, the latter being even more trivially discoverable and selectable by an attacker.
Older version lacking a specific hardening feature (rate limiting) added later, versus older version containing a fully-reintroduced, previously-patched vulnerability (a more severe variant).
mitigation: Establish and enforce a strict deprecation timeline for older API versions, actually decommissioning them rather than leaving them indefinitely reachable for backward compatibility.
Where an older version must remain temporarily available, backport all security fixes and hardening improvements to it as a mandatory part of the release process, not an optional afterthought.
Monitor and alert on traffic to deprecated API versions specifically, since sustained or unusual use of an old version is itself a signal worth investigating.

Where feasible, apply security-relevant middleware (rate limiting, input validation) at a layer shared across all versions (an API gateway) rather than duplicated per-version, so a fix or improvement automatically applies everywhere at once.

API-019.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman) and a valid test account's authentication token. Access to the API's documentation or the application's own UI to compare against the raw API response.
API-019.whatItIs: An endpoint sends back the entire underlying data record in its response. That includes internal fields never meant for the outside world — password hashes, internal IDs, other users' data mixed in, or internal status flags. The app relies on its own screen simply not displaying those extra fields, rather than the API only sending back what is actually needed.
API-019.rootCause: It's simpler during development to just send back the whole backend data record than to carefully define exactly what each endpoint should return. The assumption that 'the app just won't show the extra fields' ignores that anyone — not just the official app — can look directly at the raw API response and see everything that's actually in it.
API-019.impact: Any caller can pull sensitive internal fields straight out of the response, whatever the official app chooses to display. That can include password hashes, which may be crackable offline, internal identifiers useful for planning further attacks, and other users' data embedded inside what appears to be a single-user object. The interface hiding a field is not the same as the API withholding it.
stepsToIdentify: Capture full, raw API responses for a representative set of endpoints using a test account, and compare the complete response structure against what the application's own UI actually displays.

Flag any additional fields present in the raw response that aren't shown in the UI, particularly ones that look sensitive (containing "hash", "internal", "ssn", or similar naming patterns) or that reference other users' data.
For any suspicious field, assess its actual sensitivity and confirm it's genuinely populated with real, non-null sensitive data rather than being an always-empty placeholder field.

Cross-reference this finding against the more specific property-level-authorization finding where the excess field is not just present but also writable, which is a materially more severe combined finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes full raw API response inspection using the provided test account.
Capture the complete raw response for a representative set of endpoints.
Identify and document every field present in the response but not surfaced by the official UI, especially any containing sensitive data.

Where a password hash or other crackable/sensitive value is found, note its format (bcrypt, MD5, etc.) as part of the severity assessment, without necessarily performing offline cracking unless that's separately in scope.
Document each over-exposed field, its data sensitivity, and the specific endpoint(s) affected.

examplePayloads.label: Capture and inspect a full raw API response for excess fields
Compare the raw response structure against the application's displayed fields
examplePayloads.command: # manually cross-reference every key in the jq-formatted response against what's rendered in the application's own profile/account UI

variants: Excess data exposure on a single-object endpoint (a user profile) versus a list/collection endpoint, where the excess-field problem is multiplied across every returned record.

Excess field present but populated with a genuinely sensitive value (a password hash) versus an internal-but-low-sensitivity field (an internal database row ID) — both are findings, but severity differs materially.
mitigation: Define and maintain an explicit response schema/DTO for every endpoint, returning only the specific fields the calling client genuinely needs, rather than serializing the full backend data model.
Never include password hashes or other raw credential material in any API response under any circumstance, regardless of whether the field is displayed by the official client.
Apply a consistent, centrally-enforced response-filtering pattern across the API rather than relying on ad hoc, per-endpoint field selection.
Include response-schema validation in automated testing to catch any newly-introduced excess field before release.

API-020.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) capable of sending a streaming upload/request with a deliberately mismatched or manipulated `Content-Length` header, or with chunked-transfer-encoding used to disguise the actual data volume sent.
API-020.whatItIs: An endpoint that accepts a large upload or a stream of data trusts a value the client itself reports (saying 'this is how much data I'm sending') to decide how much space to prepare, instead of independently tracking and capping how much data actually arrives. That lets a client lie about the size, or just keep streaming an effectively unlimited amount of data, exhausting the server's memory or storage.
API-020.rootCause: Handling large uploads and data streams safely is more complex than handling a fixed-size request. The common shortcut is checking the size the client claims rather than counting bytes as they actually arrive. A correct implementation counts independently and cuts the connection the moment a real limit is reached, whatever the client declared.
API-020.impact: An attacker gets the server to allocate resources based on a size the client claims but nothing verifies. Alternatively they stream an effectively unlimited amount of data without ever declaring a size upfront. Either way the server's memory, disk or processing capacity is exhausted, and legitimate users are denied service.
stepsToIdentify: Identify streaming/large-upload API endpoints and review whether size enforcement (if any) is documented as based on the `Content-Length` header versus independently-tracked actual bytes received.
Send a request with a `Content-Length` header value smaller than the actual body sent, and separately, one larger than the actual body sent, observing how the server handles each mismatch.

Where chunked transfer encoding is supported, attempt to stream a very large amount of data without declaring any upfront size, and monitor server resource consumption (if authorized and observable) during the test.

Confirm whether any independent, hard size limit is enforced regardless of header claims, by continuing to stream data past whatever the header falsely declared and past what any reasonable limit should allow.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes streaming/large-upload resource-exhaustion testing against the target endpoint, agreeing a safe, bounded test approach given the shared-infrastructure risk.
Send a request with a deliberately mismatched `Content-Length` header and observe the server's handling.
Where chunked encoding is supported, attempt a bounded, agreed-size streaming test that exceeds any documented/expected limit, monitoring for resource exhaustion indicators.
Document whether the server correctly enforces an independent, actual-bytes-received limit or relies solely on the client-supplied header/declared size.
Stop testing well before genuinely impacting shared infrastructure availability, and report the finding based on the bounded evidence gathered.

examplePayloads.label: Send a request with a Content-Length smaller than the actual body
Stream data via chunked transfer encoding without declaring an upfront size
Monitor server resource consumption during a bounded, authorized streaming test
examplePayloads.command: # with client authorization: monitor server-side CPU/memory/disk metrics during the bounded test request

variants: Content-Length mismatch used to cause a buffer over-allocation (undersized header, oversized actual body) versus chunked-encoding abuse to bypass any upfront-size-based limit entirely.
Resource exhaustion targeting memory (in-memory buffering of the full upload before processing) versus disk space (writing an unbounded amount of streamed data directly to disk).
mitigation: Enforce a maximum upload/request size based on independently-tracked actual bytes received as they arrive, terminating the connection immediately upon exceeding the limit, regardless of what the `Content-Length` header or chunked-encoding stream claims.

Apply the size limit at the earliest possible point in the request-handling pipeline (ideally at a reverse proxy/load balancer layer) rather than only within application-level code, reducing the resource cost of enforcement itself.
Stream large uploads directly to bounded, monitored storage rather than buffering the full content in memory before processing.
Apply per-client/per-account upload-volume rate limiting in addition to a per-request size limit, to catch abuse patterns using many smaller, individually-compliant requests.

API-021.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) with GraphQL-specific tooling (InQL, GraphQL Voyager, or a manual query-crafting approach) and a valid test account's authentication token if the target endpoint requires it.
API-021.whatItIs: GraphQL lets a client ask for deeply nested, related data in one request, or bundle many separate requests into one. Without a limit on how deep or how large that request can be, a single carefully crafted query can force the server into a hugely disproportionate amount of work behind the scenes. The request itself looks trivial on the surface, which is what makes the mismatch dangerous.
API-021.rootCause: GraphQL's flexibility — letting a client specify exactly what related data it wants and how deeply nested — is also exactly what makes it risky, because without an explicit, enforced limit on how deep or complex a single query can be, the structure of the data itself defines the maximum possible cost of one client-crafted request. Setting that limit is a separate, deliberate step that's easy to skip when first setting up a GraphQL service.
API-021.impact: A single request of ordinary size can trigger a hugely disproportionate amount of backend and database work. One attacker with a normal account — or none at all, on a public endpoint — can exhaust resources and take the service down. Compared with a traditional flooding attack it requires almost no bandwidth, which also makes it harder to spot as an attack.
stepsToIdentify: Use introspection (if enabled) or documentation to understand the GraphQL schema's relational structure, identifying types with circular or deeply-nestable relationships (e.g. a user who has posts, each post has comments, each comment has an author who has posts...).
Craft a query nesting several levels deep through such a relational chain and measure the response time/apparent server load relative to a simple, shallow query.

Separately, test query batching/aliasing by submitting many operations (or many aliased instances of the same expensive query) within a single request, checking whether any batch-size limit is enforced.

Confirm whether any query-complexity/depth-limiting middleware is present at all by progressively increasing nesting depth/batch size and observing whether the server ever rejects a query for being too complex, versus processing an arbitrarily deep/large one.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes GraphQL query-complexity/depth and batching abuse testing against the target endpoint, with an agreed, bounded approach given the resource-exhaustion risk to shared infrastructure.
Craft a deeply-nested query through an identified circular/recursive relational chain in the schema.
Submit the query with progressively increasing nesting depth, carefully monitoring response time growth, and stop well before genuinely impacting availability.

Separately, test query batching by submitting a bounded number of aliased, moderately-expensive query instances in a single request and observe the aggregate processing-time impact relative to a single instance.
Document the maximum nesting depth/batch size that was processed without any complexity-limiting rejection, and the corresponding disproportionate resource-cost evidence gathered.

examplePayloads.label: Craft a deeply-nested query through a circular relational chain
examplePayloads.command: curl -s -X POST https://api.target.com/graphql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":"{ user(id:1) { posts { comments { author { posts { comments { author { id } } } } } } } }"}'

examplePayloads.label: Test query batching/aliasing for a bounded resource-cost multiplication
examplePayloads.command: curl -s -X POST https://api.target.com/graphql -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":"{ a1: expensiveQuery a2: expensiveQuery a3: expensiveQuery a4: expensiveQuery a5: expensiveQuery }"}'

examplePayloads.label: Automated GraphQL query-complexity fuzzing

variants: Query-depth abuse via a naturally circular schema relationship, versus alias-based batching abuse that repeats an expensive (but not necessarily deeply-nested) query many times within one request.
Abuse reachable pre-authentication on a public GraphQL endpoint versus only reachable by an authenticated user, affecting real-world exploitability and severity.
mitigation: Implement and enforce a maximum query-depth limit, rejecting any query exceeding a reasonable, application-appropriate nesting threshold.
Implement query-complexity/cost analysis (assigning a computed cost to each field/resolver and enforcing a maximum total cost per query) for more precise control than depth-limiting alone.
Limit the number of aliased operations/batched queries permitted in a single request.
Disable introspection in production (overlapping with the debug-endpoint-exposure finding) to reduce an attacker's ability to easily discover exploitable relational structures in the schema.

API-022.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) and a content-discovery/fuzzing tool (ffuf, gobuster) with a wordlist targeting common internal/gateway route-naming patterns. Access to any client-side code (a JavaScript bundle, a mobile app) that might reference internal route names.
API-022.whatItIs: The company's API gateway routes to an internal-only backend endpoint that was never meant to be public and isn't listed in any public documentation — but it's still reachable by anyone who happens to discover its path, because 'not documented' was mistakenly treated as the same thing as 'protected.'
API-022.rootCause: This internal route was added to the gateway for a legitimate internal reason — an admin tool, a partner integration, a testing convenience — without also adding a real access restriction limiting who can actually reach it. Leaving it out of public docs was relied on as if that were an actual security control, instead of pairing it with real authentication or a network restriction.
API-022.impact: Any outside caller who discovers the undocumented path can call it directly. Finding it is not difficult: it may be referenced in the client-side code bundle, turn up in a fuzzing scan, or simply be guessable from the naming patterns visible in the documented API. What it reaches may be administrative functionality or internal data never intended to be externally callable.
stepsToIdentify: Inspect any available client-side code (JavaScript bundles, a mobile app's decompiled network-call references) for API paths not present in the official, public API documentation.
Run a content-discovery/fuzzing scan against the gateway's base path using a wordlist built from common internal/admin/gateway naming conventions and any path fragments observed in client-side code.

For each discovered undocumented route, test whether it's reachable without authentication, or with only the same authentication level as an ordinary external API consumer, rather than requiring genuine internal-network access or elevated internal credentials.
Where reachable, assess what functionality/data the route exposes to correctly scope the finding's severity.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes content-discovery scanning and interaction with any discovered undocumented gateway routes.
Run the fuzzing scan and review client-side code for undocumented route candidates.
For each candidate found reachable, document what functionality/data it exposes and the authentication level (if any) actually enforced.
Where the route exposes genuinely sensitive internal functionality, demonstrate a benign, non-destructive interaction (if authorized) to confirm real exploitability.
Document each discovered undocumented route, its reachability, and its exposed functionality/data.

examplePayloads.label: Fuzz the gateway for common internal/admin route naming patterns
Search client-side JavaScript for undocumented API path references
Test reachability of a discovered undocumented route

variants: Undocumented route discovered via client-side code inspection (indicating it's actually called by some legitimate client, just not publicly documented) versus discovered purely via fuzzing (indicating it may be entirely orphaned/forgotten functionality).
Undocumented route requiring the same authentication as the public API (lower severity, since at least some access control exists) versus requiring no authentication whatsoever.
mitigation: Maintain a complete, accurate inventory of every route configured on the API gateway, explicitly classifying each as public, partner-restricted, or internal-only — never relying on omission from public documentation as a substitute for actual access control.

Restrict internal-only routes to genuine internal network reachability (not exposed through the same publicly-reachable gateway listener at all) or, at minimum, a separate, strong authentication requirement distinct from the public API's.
Periodically audit the gateway's full routing configuration against the maintained inventory to catch any route that's drifted out of its intended classification or been forgotten entirely.
Include undocumented-route discovery (via fuzzing) as a standing check in routine API security assessments, since this is a common and easy-to-overlook gap.

API-023.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) capable of sending a raw JSON request body with intentionally duplicated keys. Knowledge (or the ability to infer) of whether any intermediate component — a WAF, an API gateway, or a validation layer — parses the same JSON body separately from the backend application.
API-023.whatItIs: A request body with a duplicate field (technically allowed by the JSON format, even though how it should be handled isn't strictly defined) gets read differently by two different parts of the system — say, a security filter reads the first occurrence of that field while the actual application reads the last one (or vice versa). That mismatch lets an attacker craft a request where the value getting checked isn't the same value that actually gets used.
API-023.rootCause: The JSON format doesn't specify one single correct way to handle a duplicate field, so different tools parsing the same request — a security filter versus the actual application — can and do interpret it differently. If a security check happens on one interpretation while the real processing happens on a different one, an attacker can exploit that gap between the two.
API-023.impact: An attacker sends the same field twice. The first copy carries an innocuous value, which is what the validating component inspects and approves. The second copy carries the real payload, and that is the one the application actually uses. The value that got checked and the value that gets used are different, which is precisely how the validation layer is defeated.
stepsToIdentify: Identify request-processing components in the chain that might parse the same JSON body independently (a WAF, an API gateway performing validation, versus the backend application itself).
Craft a request with a duplicated key, where the first occurrence carries an innocuous, validation-passing value and the second occurrence carries a different, more sensitive value.

Submit the request and observe which value the backend application actually acts upon (via the resulting response or side effect), compared to what a validation layer would have inspected if it takes the opposite occurrence.
Where a divergence is confirmed, assess what security-relevant field could realistically be smuggled this way (a role/permission field, an ownership ID) to determine the practical impact.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes duplicate-JSON-key testing against the target API's request-processing chain.
Identify a security-relevant field (a role, a resource-ownership ID) processed by the endpoint under test.
Craft a request with that field duplicated — an innocuous first value, followed by a different, unauthorized second value for the same key.
Submit the request and confirm which value the backend actually processed, based on the observable response or resulting state change.
Where the backend processed the smuggled (second/attacker-intended) value despite an intervening validation layer, document the exact parser-differential behavior and resulting bypass achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Send a request with a duplicated key carrying divergent values
Confirm which value the backend actually applied

variants: Duplicate-key confusion between a WAF/gateway validation layer and the backend application, versus between two different backend microservices in a chained-processing architecture that each parse the same forwarded body independently.
Duplicate-key confusion exploited for an authorization bypass (smuggling a role/permission field) versus for a business-logic bypass (smuggling a price/quantity field past a validation check).
mitigation: Standardize on a single, consistent JSON-parsing behavior for duplicate keys across every component in the request-processing chain, ideally by using the same parsing library/version everywhere a given request body is inspected.
Reject requests containing duplicate keys outright at the earliest point in the processing chain, rather than attempting to resolve the ambiguity permissively.

Where multiple components must independently parse the same body (a WAF and a backend application), periodically test for exactly this class of parser-differential behavior as part of routine security assessments.

Apply the security-relevant validation check as close as possible to the point of actual use (ideally within the same component/parsing pass) to eliminate the risk of a differing interpretation being introduced by an intermediate layer.

API-024.prerequisites: Access to the organization's API documentation, gateway configuration, and change-management records (with appropriate authorization), and content-discovery/fuzzing tooling to independently corroborate the documented inventory against what's actually deployed.
API-024.whatItIs: The organization doesn't have a complete, accurate, up-to-date list of every API version, environment, and endpoint it's actually running. That means security reviews and access-control decisions get made against an incomplete picture — some deployed APIs (an old version, a testing environment accidentally left reachable from the internet) end up outside of any routine security process, simply because nobody has a record that they even exist.
API-024.rootCause: The set of APIs an organization actually runs naturally grows and fragments over time as new versions ship, test environments get spun up, and partner-specific variants get created — without a disciplined, continuously maintained inventory tracking all of it. Keeping this list current is an ongoing job, not a one-time setup task, and it's easy for it to fall behind as things change faster than anyone's tracking them.
API-024.impact: APIs missing from the inventory receive no routine security attention at all — no patching, no access-control review, no deprecation — because the process that governs everything else simply does not know they exist. That creates a growing blind spot with an unfortunate property: the highest-risk assets, such as an old vulnerable version or a forgotten internet-reachable staging environment, are the least likely to be caught, precisely because being forgotten is what made them risky.
stepsToIdentify: Obtain the organization's documented API inventory (from internal documentation, an API gateway's configured routes, or a service-catalog tool) as the starting baseline.

Independently corroborate this baseline via external reconnaissance — subdomain enumeration, certificate-transparency log review, and content-discovery scanning — to identify any API-shaped endpoint not present in the documented inventory.

For each discrepancy found (an endpoint that exists but isn't documented, or a documented endpoint that no longer actually exists), assess its current security posture independently, since it likely hasn't received routine attention.
Interview the platform/API-management team on their current inventory-maintenance process to understand whether gaps are a one-time historical accumulation or an ongoing, systemic process gap.
exploitationSteps: This finding is primarily identified through inventory reconciliation and external reconnaissance rather than actively exploited by the tester, since the finding itself is a process/governance gap rather than a directly technical vulnerability.
Confirm scope authorizes external reconnaissance (subdomain enumeration, certificate-transparency review, content-discovery scanning) against the target organization's domains.
Compile the list of discovered API-shaped endpoints not present in the documented inventory.

For any discovered, undocumented, and reachable API found to also carry a specific technical vulnerability (weaker authentication, an old, vulnerable version), cross-reference and report that as a chained, concrete finding illustrating the inventory gap's real-world consequence.
Document the full reconciliation results (documented-but-nonexistent, and undocumented-but-existent) as the primary deliverable for this finding.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate subdomains as an independent API-surface discovery method
Review certificate-transparency logs for API-shaped hostnames not in the documented inventory
Content-discovery scan against a discovered, undocumented candidate host

variants: An old, deprecated API version still deployed and reachable but dropped from current documentation, versus an entirely separate staging/pre-production environment inadvertently left internet-reachable and never included in any inventory at all.
A partner-specific API variant created for one specific integration, documented only in that partner's own records rather than the organization's central inventory.
mitigation: Establish and maintain a single, authoritative, continuously-updated API inventory covering every version, environment, and variant, ideally auto-populated from the API gateway/service-mesh configuration rather than manually maintained documentation.
Integrate inventory reconciliation (comparing documented inventory against actual external reconnaissance results) as a recurring, scheduled process rather than a one-time exercise.
Apply the same security-review, patching, and access-control rigor to every API found in the inventory, regardless of its apparent age or perceived low-usage status.
Decommission genuinely obsolete API versions/environments promptly rather than leaving them reachable indefinitely once they fall out of active, documented use.

API-025.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) and valid credentials/tokens for at least two separate test accounts. A shared or CDN-fronted caching layer in front of the API (a CDN, a reverse-proxy cache) to test cache-key behavior against.
API-025.whatItIs: A response containing data specific to one logged-in user — like a personal dashboard or order history — gets cached by an intermediate system (a CDN or proxy) using a cache key that doesn't account for who's actually asking, usually because the cache key is based only on the web address, ignoring the login token or cookie that determines whose data is actually in the response. So a second, completely different user requesting that same address gets served the first user's cached, personal data.
API-025.rootCause: Caching systems are typically set up to key on the URL alone for efficiency. Unless a response is explicitly marked as private and non-cacheable, or the cache is specifically told to also factor in the login token, the caching layer has no way to know this particular response is personal rather than something generic that's safe to share — it just serves back whatever it last cached for that address.
API-025.impact: A second user requesting the same URL receives the first user's cached response, complete with their account data and session-specific content. From the caching layer's point of view the two requests look identical, because it never considered who was asking. This is an entirely accidental cross-user data leak, and it affects every user who requests that URL after someone else's personalised response was stored.
stepsToIdentify: Identify API endpoints returning personalized, per-user data and check the response headers for `Cache-Control`/`Vary` directives indicating caching behavior.

Using test account A, request the endpoint and confirm the response is cached (via a `Cache-Status`/`X-Cache: HIT` header on a subsequent identical request, or via observed response timing consistent with a cache hit).
Using test account B's credentials, request the exact same URL and check whether the response returned is actually account B's data or account A's previously-cached data.
Where the caching layer is a CDN, review its configuration (if accessible) for whether the cache key includes the `Authorization` header/session cookie, or is based purely on URL/query string.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cross-account cache-poisoning-style testing using the provided test accounts against the target caching layer.
Using test account A, request the target endpoint and confirm the response is served from cache on a repeat request.
Using test account B's authentication, request the identical URL and inspect the returned data.
Confirm whether account B received account A's cached, personalized data rather than their own.
Document the exact endpoint, the caching layer's configuration gap (missing private/no-store directive, or a cache key not varying on identity), and the confirmed cross-account data leak.

examplePayloads.label: Request an endpoint as account A and confirm caching behavior
Repeat the identical request as account B and inspect the returned data

variants: Cache-poisoning-style cross-user leak via a shared CDN, versus a similar issue at a local browser/proxy cache level due to a missing `private` Cache-Control directive, which affects a narrower, single-user scope but is still a finding worth noting.
Personalized data leaked via full response caching versus only a specific, sensitive header (a `Set-Cookie` or session token) being inadvertently cached and replayed to a different user.
mitigation: Mark every response containing per-user, personalized data with `Cache-Control: private, no-store` (or the equivalent directive appropriate to the caching infrastructure in use), explicitly preventing shared/intermediate caching.

Where caching of personalized content is genuinely desired for performance reasons, configure the cache to vary its key on the authentication identity (the `Authorization` header or session cookie), ensuring each user gets their own distinct cache entry.
Periodically test caching behavior for exactly this cross-account leak pattern as part of routine API security assessments, since CDN/cache configuration changes can silently reintroduce this issue.

Apply cache-control headers via a centrally-enforced middleware/policy rather than per-endpoint configuration, reducing the chance of a newly-added personalized endpoint missing the appropriate directive.

API-026.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) and access to the target's webhook-configuration or webhook-delivery-log functionality (via a test account) to observe generated webhook IDs.
API-026.whatItIs: Webhook records (representing event subscriptions or delivered event data) are given simple, sequential ID numbers, and an endpoint that looks one up by ID doesn't check that the person asking actually owns that specific webhook. An attacker can just count up or down through IDs and access or tamper with other customers' webhook settings or delivered event data.
API-026.rootCause: This is really the same underlying problem as a broken ownership check, just specifically applied to webhooks. Webhook records are often treated as a lower-profile, less obviously sensitive data type than core business data, so the same ownership check applied elsewhere in the API may have simply been overlooked for this particular feature.
API-026.impact: An attacker walks through sequential webhook IDs to reach other customers' configurations. That reveals destination URLs and, where included, the shared secret used to verify that a webhook genuinely came from the platform. The delivered event payloads are exposed too, and those routinely carry the same sensitive business data as the main API — pushing that data to the customer is the entire point of a webhook.
stepsToIdentify: Using a test account, create or trigger a webhook subscription/event and note the resulting resource's ID, checking whether it's sequential/predictable.
Using the same test account (to establish a baseline of ownership), request the webhook resource by its known ID and confirm normal, expected access.
Increment or decrement the ID and re-request, checking whether a different, presumably-other-customer's webhook resource is returned rather than an access-denied response.
Where accessible, assess what data the returned webhook resource contains (destination URL, signing secret, event payload) to size the impact.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes sequential-ID enumeration testing against the target's webhook-related endpoints using the provided test account.
Create/trigger a test webhook resource and note its assigned ID.
Request the resource at IDs adjacent to (but different from) the test account's own known ID.
Confirm whether a different resource — belonging to another account — is returned, and document what specific data it contains.

Document the exact endpoint, the ID-predictability pattern, and the confirmed cross-account access achieved, without retaining or acting on any real other-customer data beyond what's needed as evidence.

examplePayloads.label: Request a webhook resource by its known, test-account-owned ID
Increment/decrement the ID and re-request to test for cross-account access
examplePayloads.command: for id in 4999 5000 5002 5003; do curl -s https://api.target.com/webhooks/$id -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>"; done

variants: Sequential ID exposure on webhook *configuration* resources (revealing destination URLs/secrets) versus on individual delivered *event* records (revealing actual business data payloads) — both are findings, with the latter often carrying more directly sensitive business data.
The same underlying BOLA root cause but affecting a webhook-signing-secret specifically, which compounds the finding by also enabling forged webhook delivery to another customer's endpoint.
mitigation: Apply the same object-level ownership authorization check to webhook-related endpoints as is applied to core business-object endpoints, scoping every query to the authenticated caller's own webhook resources.
Use non-sequential, non-guessable identifiers (UUIDs) for webhook resources as a defense-in-depth measure.

Include webhook-related endpoints explicitly in the standard BOLA test-case checklist for every API assessment, since they're a commonly overlooked resource type relative to more obviously central business objects.

Treat webhook signing secrets with the same protection rigor as any other credential, ensuring they're never exposed even to the legitimate owning account through an ordinary read endpoint (only shown once at creation, for example).

API-027.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) and a valid test account for an API endpoint that supports idempotency keys (commonly a payment/transaction-creation endpoint).
API-027.whatItIs: An endpoint that accepts a client-provided 'idempotency key' — meant to safely let a client retry a request without accidentally repeating its effect, like avoiding a double charge on a network retry — doesn't properly tie that key to the specific person and specific request it was meant for. An attacker can reuse or guess someone else's key, either replaying their transaction, or having their own, different request incorrectly treated as a repeat of someone else's.
API-027.rootCause: For this feature to work safely, the key needs to be tied to both who's using it and (ideally) what the actual request contains — so the same key from a different person, or the same key reused with different data, gets correctly treated as a separate, new request. If the key is instead treated as one global value with no connection to who submitted it, the safety guarantee it's supposed to provide breaks down entirely across accounts.
API-027.impact: There are two ways this fails, depending on the implementation. An attacker who guesses or observes someone else's idempotency key can replay their transaction, potentially triggering a duplicate charge in the victim's name. Or they submit their own request carrying someone else's key, and the server returns that other person's transaction result instead of processing theirs. Either outcome defeats the exact financial integrity the mechanism exists to guarantee.
stepsToIdentify: Identify endpoints supporting client-supplied idempotency keys (commonly documented explicitly, given the feature's opt-in nature for API consumers).
Using test account A, submit a request with a specific idempotency key and note the resulting transaction/response.

Using test account B, submit a request with the same idempotency key (but different request parameters) and observe whether the server correctly processes it as a distinct new operation, or incorrectly returns account A's cached result, or otherwise behaves unexpectedly.
Check whether idempotency keys are scoped per-account in the server's storage/lookup logic, or stored in a single, global namespace shared across all callers.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes cross-account idempotency-key testing using the provided test accounts against a designated test transaction endpoint.
Using test account A, submit a request with a specific, known idempotency key value.
Using test account B, submit a request with the identical idempotency key but different parameters.
Confirm the server's behavior — whether it correctly processes account B's distinct request, or incorrectly conflates it with account A's prior operation.
Document the exact endpoint, the confirmed cross-account idempotency-key scoping gap, and the resulting business-logic impact demonstrated.

examplePayloads.label: Submit a request as account A with a specific idempotency key
Submit a request as account B reusing the same idempotency key with different parameters

variants: Idempotency key not scoped by caller identity at all (a global namespace) versus scoped by caller but not by request-parameter hash, allowing the same authenticated user to reuse a key across genuinely different transactions and have the second incorrectly treated as a duplicate of the first.

Predictable/guessable idempotency keys (if the client is expected to generate them but the server doesn't validate sufficient entropy) enabling an attacker to preemptively guess and interfere with another user's upcoming request.
mitigation: Scope idempotency-key storage/lookup by both the authenticated caller's identity and a hash of the actual request parameters, ensuring the same key value from a different caller (or with different parameters) is never conflated with another request.
Set a reasonable expiry window on stored idempotency keys, after which the same key can be reused for a genuinely new operation, bounding the storage/lookup scope over time.
Document and enforce a minimum entropy/format requirement for client-supplied idempotency keys to reduce the risk of accidental or intentional collision.
Include idempotency-key cross-account test cases in the standard regression-test suite for any endpoint supporting this feature.

API-028.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) and valid credentials/tokens for at least two separate test accounts, each with their own set of nested/child resources (e.g. each account having its own projects, and each project having its own documents).
API-028.whatItIs: An endpoint uses a nested web address — like account/project/document — and correctly checks that you own the account, but never checks that the project and document IDs you supplied actually belong to that same account. You can keep your own valid account ID but swap in someone else's project or document ID, and the request still goes through against data that isn't yours.
API-028.rootCause: Checking ownership through a chain of nested items (does this document belong to this project, does this project belong to this account) is more work to get right than checking just one level. Often only the first, most obvious check gets built — the assumption being that if you own the account, anything nested underneath it must also be yours — but that assumption is never actually verified.
API-028.impact: A logged-in user keeps their own valid account ID in the path but swaps the nested resource ID — a project, a document — for someone else's. The request succeeds. This variant is easy to miss in testing, because checking only the obvious single-ID substitution passes; catching it requires systematically trying every combination of matching and mismatched path segments.
stepsToIdentify: Using test account A, create a nested resource (a project, then a document within that project) and note the full compound path with all resulting IDs.
Using test account B, create an equivalent, separate nested resource and note its own full compound path/IDs.
Using test account A's authentication (and A's own top-level account ID in the path), substitute account B's nested project/document ID into the path and submit the request.
Confirm whether the server processes the request against account B's nested resource despite the mismatched ownership chain, or correctly rejects it.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes nested-resource-ownership testing using the provided test accounts.
Create parallel nested resources under both test account A and test account B.
Using account A's authentication and its own top-level account ID, substitute account B's nested resource ID(s) into the compound path.
Submit the request and confirm whether account B's nested resource is returned or modified, despite the path's top-level segment belonging to account A.
Document the exact endpoint, the specific nested-ownership check gap, and the resulting cross-account access achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Create parallel nested resources under two separate test accounts
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s -X POST https://api.target.com/accounts/A100/projects -H "Authorization: Bearer <account-A-token>" -d '{"name":"Project A"}'
curl -s -X POST https://api.target.com/accounts/B200/projects -H "Authorization: Bearer <account-B-token>" -d '{"name":"Project B"}'

examplePayloads.label: Substitute account B's nested project ID while authenticated and path-scoped as account A

variants: Mismatch tested at the project-level nesting (account A's ID + account B's project ID) versus a deeper, document-level nesting mismatch (correct account and project IDs, but a document ID belonging to a different project entirely) — both are variants of the same missing full-chain verification.
The nested-ownership gap affecting a read operation versus a write/delete operation on the mismatched nested resource, the latter being materially more severe.
mitigation: Verify the complete ownership chain for every segment of a compound/nested resource path — confirm the project belongs to the specified account, and the document belongs to the specified project, not just that the caller owns the top-level account.

Where feasible, simplify the authorization model by deriving nested resource scope directly from the authenticated caller's own account context server-side, rather than trusting any nested ID supplied in the path at all.

Include full-chain, multi-segment ownership test cases (testing every combination of matching/mismatched path segments, not just the single most obvious substitution) in the standard BOLA regression-test suite.
Apply a centralized, reusable nested-resource-authorization helper/middleware across every compound-path endpoint rather than reimplementing the chain-verification logic ad hoc per endpoint.

API-029.prerequisites: Read access to the target API's logging/monitoring configuration and, where available, sample log output (with client authorization). Ability to trigger representative security-relevant events (a failed login, a BOLA-style access attempt, an authorization failure) against a test environment to observe whether they're logged.
API-029.whatItIs: The API doesn't log security-relevant events at all, or logs them without enough detail — missing who made the request, from where, or what exactly they did — to actually investigate anything after the fact. And no alerts are set up for suspicious patterns, like a burst of failed logins or repeated failed attempts to access many different account IDs in a row (a sign someone's probing for an ownership-check bug). An attack in progress, or one that already happened, might go completely unnoticed.
API-029.rootCause: Logging usually gets built with performance and error-tracking in mind rather than security detection. Nobody asks what a brute-force attempt would actually look like in these logs. Without that question being asked during design, the logs that do exist frequently fail to capture the specific signal an investigator or an automated alert would need.
API-029.impact: An attacker's activity leaves no usable trace, whether they succeeded or failed. The organisation cannot detect the attack while it is happening. Afterwards it cannot establish scope — which records were touched, by whom, when. And it cannot support any legal, regulatory or breach-notification process, since all of those depend on being able to reconstruct what actually occurred.
stepsToIdentify: Review the API's logging configuration and sample log output for the presence (or absence) of key security-relevant fields: caller identity, source IP, timestamp, the specific resource/action, and the outcome (success/failure).

Trigger a representative set of security-relevant test events (a failed login, a deliberately unauthorized object-access attempt using a test account) against a test environment and confirm whether each is actually captured in the logs with sufficient detail.

Check whether any alerting/detection rule exists for common attack patterns (authentication brute-force, BOLA-style ID enumeration, a burst of 403/401 responses from a single caller) by reviewing the monitoring/SIEM configuration if accessible.
Assess log retention duration and whether logs are protected from tampering/deletion by an attacker who might gain sufficient access to cover their tracks.
exploitationSteps: This finding is primarily identified through configuration and log-content review rather than actively exploited, since the finding itself is a detection/response-readiness gap rather than a directly exploitable technical vulnerability.
Confirm scope authorizes triggering representative security-relevant test events against a test environment for log-capture verification.
Trigger each representative event (failed login, unauthorized access attempt) and immediately check whether it appears in the logs with adequate detail.
Where alerting is claimed to exist, trigger a pattern that should reasonably fire an alert (a burst of failed logins) and confirm whether an actual alert is generated and reaches a monitoring team.
Document each specific logging/alerting gap found, prioritized by how central the missing coverage is to detecting a realistic, high-impact attack scenario.

examplePayloads.label: Trigger a failed authentication attempt and check for log capture
examplePayloads.command:
curl -s -X POST https://api.target.com/login -d '{"username":"test","password":"wrong"}'
# then check with the client whether this attempt appears in their logging/SIEM system

examplePayloads.label: Trigger a deliberate, bounded unauthorized-access attempt for log-capture verification
examplePayloads.command: curl -s https://api.target.com/orders/99999 -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>"  # an object ID the test account doesn't own, then verify with the client whether this 403/404 attempt is logged with caller identity

variants: Logging present but missing key fields (caller identity, source IP) needed to actually investigate an incident, versus no security-relevant logging at all for certain event types.
Logs correctly captured but no alerting/detection rule configured against them at all, meaning the data exists but nothing surfaces it to a human or automated response process in a timely manner.
mitigation: Design logging deliberately around security-detection use cases — explicitly log every authentication attempt (success and failure), every authorization decision (especially failures), and every sensitive data-access/modification action, each with caller identity, source IP, timestamp, and outcome.

Implement alerting/detection rules for well-known attack patterns (authentication brute-force, high-volume authorization failures suggesting enumeration, unusual access-pattern spikes) tied to the security-relevant logs.

Protect logs from tampering/deletion (write-once storage, forwarding to a separate, access-restricted logging system) so an attacker who gains some level of access can't simply erase evidence of their activity.
Define and enforce an adequate log-retention period aligned with the organization's incident-response and any applicable regulatory requirements.

API-030.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite/Postman) and a valid test account's authentication token. Access to the full object schema (via documentation, introspection, or a full raw response) to identify fields beyond what the legitimate create/update request normally includes.
API-030.whatItIs: An endpoint that creates or updates something — a user profile, an order — takes the entire request body and applies it directly to the underlying data record, with no explicit list of which fields are actually allowed to be set that way. That means a caller can sneak in extra fields that were never meant to be editable — like a role, a permission flag, a price, or an 'isAdmin' setting — and have them silently accepted, even though the real app interface never shows those as changeable.
API-030.rootCause: Many frameworks make it very convenient to take a whole request and apply it directly to a data record. That makes building an endpoint quick. It also means every field on that record becomes settable by anyone who includes it in their request, whether or not that was ever intended.
API-030.impact: A caller can raise their own privileges by setting a role or permission field directly. They can alter financially meaningful values such as a price, a discount or a balance, bypassing the validated path those changes were meant to travel through. In fact any field present in the underlying data model is reachable, regardless of what the interface treats as editable. It is a direct integrity and access-control violation.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the endpoint's legitimate, documented request body structure (the fields the official UI actually sends).

Obtain the full underlying object schema (via API documentation, a full raw GET response for the same object type, or framework/ORM documentation if source access is available) to identify additional fields that exist on the object but aren't part of the legitimate request structure.
Craft a request including one or more of these additional fields (particularly any resembling a role, permission, price, or status field) alongside the legitimate expected fields.
Submit the request and confirm whether the additional field(s) were silently accepted and applied to the object, by subsequently retrieving the object and checking its current state.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes mass-assignment testing using the provided test account against the target create/update endpoint.
Capture the legitimate request body structure for a normal create/update action.
Add an additional, normally-restricted field (a role/permission flag, a price field) to the request body.
Submit the modified request and then retrieve the resulting object to confirm whether the injected field was applied.
Document the exact endpoint, the specific vulnerable field, and the resulting privilege-escalation or business-logic-manipulation impact achieved.

examplePayloads.label: Capture the legitimate request body for a normal profile-update action
Attempt mass assignment by including an additional, restricted field
Confirm whether the injected fields were applied

variants: Mass assignment enabling direct privilege escalation (a role field) versus enabling business-logic manipulation (a price/discount/balance field) — both share the same root cause but differ in the specific impact category.

Mass assignment on a create (registration) endpoint, allowing a brand-new account to be created with elevated privileges from the outset, versus on an update endpoint modifying an existing, otherwise-ordinary account.
mitigation: Explicitly allowlist the specific fields permitted for each create/update endpoint, binding only those fields from the request body to the underlying object rather than allowing automatic, unrestricted binding of the entire body.

Never expose a data model's full field set directly to request-binding logic; use a dedicated, narrower input schema/DTO per endpoint reflecting exactly what that specific operation should be allowed to set.
Apply the same allowlisting discipline to both creation and update endpoints for every object type, since a gap on either can independently enable this class of vulnerability.
Include mass-assignment test cases (attempting to set fields outside the documented, legitimate request structure) in routine regression testing for every create/update endpoint.

API-031.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) and a listener you control (Burp Collaborator, or a simple netcat/HTTP listener) to confirm out-of-band request delivery. A valid test account's authentication token if the vulnerable parameter sits behind an authenticated endpoint.
API-031.whatItIs: A REST endpoint takes a URL as a normal parameter — a webhook target to validate, a link to preview, an image to import — and the server requests it. With no allowlist on the destination, an attacker supplies an internal address instead: another service on the private network, a database admin panel, or the cloud provider's metadata endpoint that hands out temporary credentials to anything running on that instance.
API-031.rootCause: The endpoint treats a caller-supplied URL as ordinary data rather than as an instruction telling the server where to send a request from inside the network perimeter. Blocking this properly is harder than it first appears — a naive check on the hostname is defeated by redirects, DNS records that resolve to internal addresses, and alternate IP encodings — so a partial fix often gets written, passes a quick test, and leaves the endpoint still exploitable.
API-031.impact: An attacker makes the server issue requests on their behalf, reaching internal admin panels, databases and APIs not otherwise reachable from outside. The same technique points at the cloud provider's metadata service, which can hand back the instance's credentials. Where the endpoint reflects or processes the response, the attacker reads the results back too, turning a blind request into a readable window onto the internal network.
stepsToIdentify: Identify every API parameter that accepts a URL for a server-side fetch/validation purpose (webhook registration, file-import-by-URL, link-preview generation).

Submit a request with the URL parameter pointing to a listener you control (a Collaborator payload or netcat listener) and confirm whether an inbound request is received, proving the server fetches the URL.

Where confirmed, submit the same request with the URL parameter pointing at an internal/link-local address (a private IP range, `169.254.169.254` for cloud metadata) and observe the response for any reflected content indicating successful internal access.
Test whether any URL-scheme restriction is applied at all (does `file://` or `gopher://` also succeed) to assess the full breadth of the SSRF primitive.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes SSRF testing via the target API endpoint, including probing internal/link-local address ranges.
Submit a test request with the URL parameter pointing at a Collaborator/controlled listener to confirm out-of-band request delivery.
Submit the request with the URL parameter pointing at the cloud metadata service address (or another internal target agreed with the client) and inspect the response for reflected internal content.
Where metadata-service access is confirmed, attempt to retrieve IAM role credentials via the standard metadata-service path and validate their scope with a minimal, read-only check.
Document the exact endpoint, parameter, and the specific internal resource/metadata successfully reached.

examplePayloads.label: Confirm out-of-band request delivery via a Collaborator/controlled listener
Probe the cloud metadata service via the vulnerable parameter
Test alternate URL schemes for a broader SSRF primitive

variants: Blind SSRF (confirmable only via out-of-band interaction, no response content reflected) versus a variant that reflects fetched content directly in the response, enabling full internal-content disclosure.
SSRF via a webhook-URL-validation feature (fetching the URL once to confirm it's reachable at registration time) versus via an ongoing, repeated data-import/sync feature.
mitigation: Restrict any server-side URL-fetching functionality to an explicit allowlist of permitted schemes and destination hosts, rejecting any URL outside that allowlist.
Block requests to internal/link-local/loopback address ranges at the network egress level from the application server, as defense in depth beyond application-level allowlisting.

Where cloud metadata access is genuinely needed by the application itself, use the more restrictive Instance Metadata Service v2 (IMDSv2) with a hop-limit restriction to reduce SSRF-based credential-theft risk.

Validate and resolve the supplied URL's hostname to an IP address server-side before fetching, checking that resolved IP against the internal/link-local blocklist (to prevent a DNS-rebinding bypass of a hostname-only allowlist check).

API-032.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) capable of automating repeated requests, and a valid test account for the specific business-flow endpoint under test (a purchase/checkout flow, an account-creation flow, a coupon-redemption flow).
API-032.whatItIs: A specific, important business action exposed through the API — buying a limited item, redeeming a coupon, creating a new account, submitting a review — can be triggered over and over, very fast, by an automated script, with nothing beyond a generic, one-size-fits-all rate limit (if there's even that) stopping it. An attacker can abuse that one specific action at a speed and volume no real person ever would — buying up all the limited stock, draining a coupon budget, or mass-creating fake accounts.
API-032.rootCause: A general 'requests per minute' limit is often applied evenly across the whole API without considering that some specific actions have a much lower realistic usage rate than typical traffic. A real customer might check their order status dozens of times a day, but would never legitimately try to redeem a coupon hundreds of times in a minute. A tighter, action-specific limit reflecting that difference is a separate design decision that's easy to skip if only a generic, uniform limit was ever considered.
API-032.impact: An attacker automates the specific business flow at a scale that causes real financial harm out of all proportion to how simple the flow looks. That covers buying out limited high-demand stock for resale, draining a promotion's budget through mass coupon redemption, or mass-creating fraudulent accounts for later abuse such as fake reviews or referral fraud. A generic technical rate limit is poorly suited to stopping this, because the requests themselves are perfectly well-formed.
stepsToIdentify: Identify business-critical flows in the API with a naturally low legitimate-use-rate expectation: limited-inventory purchases, coupon/promotion redemption, account creation, review/rating submission.
For each identified flow, test whether any flow-specific rate limit or abuse-detection control exists beyond the API's generic, endpoint-agnostic rate limiting.

With authorization, automate a bounded, test-account-based repetition of the flow (e.g. repeated coupon-redemption attempts) and observe how many repetitions succeed before any flow-specific control engages.

Assess the realistic business impact of unrestricted automation at scale for each flow (financial loss from coupon abuse, inventory-exhaustion impact on legitimate customers, fraud-enablement from mass account creation).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes bounded, business-flow-specific abuse-simulation testing against a designated test environment/test account.
Automate a bounded number of repeated invocations of the identified business flow (a coupon-redemption attempt, a limited-inventory purchase attempt) using the test account.
Confirm whether the flow permits far more repetitions than a legitimate human user would ever plausibly perform, without any flow-specific rejection or challenge.

Where safe and clearly bounded, extrapolate the demonstrated automation rate to a realistic business-impact estimate (e.g. "an attacker could exhaust this month's entire coupon budget within N minutes at this rate") rather than running the abuse to its full, real-world scale.
Document the exact business flow, the absence of flow-specific abuse controls, and the extrapolated business-impact estimate.

examplePayloads.label: Test bounded repeated coupon-redemption attempts
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 50); do curl -s -X POST https://api.target.com/coupons/redeem -H "Authorization: Bearer <test-token>" -d '{"code":"PROMO2026"}'; done

examplePayloads.label: Test bounded repeated account-creation attempts for fraud-enablement assessment
examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 20); do curl -s -X POST https://api.target.com/accounts/register -d '{"email":"test'$i'@example-test-domain.com","password":"TestPass123!"}'; done

variants: Abuse of a limited-inventory purchase flow (a scalping/hoarding scenario) versus abuse of an account-creation flow (fraud/referral-bonus enablement) — both share the same root cause but differ in business-impact category.

Abuse flow reachable pre-authentication (account creation) versus only reachable by an already-authenticated user (a coupon-redemption flow tied to an existing account), affecting the realistic attacker population.
mitigation: Implement flow-specific abuse-rate limits reflecting each business flow's genuine, low legitimate-use-rate ceiling, distinct from and in addition to the API's generic, endpoint-agnostic rate limiting.
Apply CAPTCHA, proof-of-work, or an equivalent friction mechanism specifically on the highest-value abuse targets (coupon redemption, account creation) after a small number of attempts.

Monitor and alert on abnormal usage patterns for these specific business flows (a sudden spike in coupon-redemption attempts, a surge in new-account creation from related IP ranges) as a detective control complementing preventive rate limiting.

Design business-critical flows with abuse-resistance as an explicit requirement from the outset, rather than relying solely on generic, technical rate-limiting infrastructure applied uniformly across the API.

API-033.prerequisites: An API client or intercepting proxy (Burp Suite) capable of sending requests with large payloads, wide pagination/page-size parameters, or requesting expensive computed responses. A valid test account's authentication token if the target endpoint requires it.
API-033.whatItIs: One or more endpoints let a caller request or submit far more data or computation than any legitimate use would need. That might be an unlimited page-size parameter on a list endpoint, no cap on uploaded file size, or an endpoint running an expensive operation such as generating a complex report. Nothing caps how much any of it costs the server to handle.
API-033.rootCause: Setting sensible limits — maximum page size, file size and computational complexity — is a deliberate extra step beyond making an endpoint work correctly. It is commonly skipped for at least some endpoints. That happens most often with endpoints added later, or ones where the worst-case cost is not obvious from reading how the feature is normally meant to be used.
API-033.impact: One request, or a small number that are trivial to automate, consumes far more CPU, memory, database load or bandwidth than its apparent simplicity suggests. A single attacker with an ordinary account — or none at all on a public endpoint — can exhaust resources and deny service. Unlike a traditional flooding attack it needs almost no bandwidth, so it is both cheaper to run and harder to recognise.
stepsToIdentify: Identify list/collection endpoints and test whether a page-size or limit parameter can be set to an unusually large value without being capped or rejected.
Identify endpoints accepting a request payload/upload and test whether an unusually large payload is accepted without a size-limit rejection.

Identify any endpoint performing a potentially expensive server-side computation (a report, a complex filter/search) and test with parameters designed to maximize that computation's cost, measuring response time/apparent resource impact relative to a minimal-cost equivalent request.

Confirm the growth in resource cost (response time, or observable server load if authorized to monitor it) is disproportionate to the request's apparent simplicity, rather than a reasonable, expected linear cost increase.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes resource-consumption testing against the target API, with an agreed, bounded approach given the shared-infrastructure risk.
Test a list endpoint with a very large page-size parameter and confirm whether it's processed without rejection or capping.
Test an upload/payload-accepting endpoint with a large but bounded, agreed test payload size.
Test an expensive-computation endpoint with worst-case parameters, carefully measuring response time and stopping well before genuinely impacting shared infrastructure.
Document each endpoint found lacking a resource-consumption limit, the specific unbounded parameter, and the measured disproportionate resource-cost impact.

examplePayloads.label: Test an unbounded page-size parameter on a list endpoint
Test a large, bounded payload upload for size-limit enforcement
Test an expensive-computation endpoint with worst-case parameters

variants: Unbounded page-size/list-limit abuse versus unbounded payload-size abuse versus unbounded computational-complexity abuse — each is a distinct manifestation of the same missing-resource-limit root cause, and an API may exhibit one, several, or all of them across different endpoints.
Resource exhaustion reachable pre-authentication on a public endpoint versus only reachable by an authenticated user, affecting real-world exploitability and severity.
mitigation: Enforce a hard maximum page-size/limit on every list/collection endpoint, rejecting or silently capping any request exceeding it.
Enforce a maximum request-payload size at the earliest point in the request-handling pipeline (ideally at a reverse proxy/gateway layer).

For endpoints performing expensive computation, enforce reasonable bounds on the parameters that drive that computation's cost (a maximum date range, a maximum number of grouping dimensions) and consider async/queued processing with a result-polling pattern for genuinely expensive, legitimate use cases rather than a synchronous, unbounded request.

Apply per-client/per-account resource-consumption rate limiting (not just request-count rate limiting) to catch abuse patterns using many smaller, individually-compliant-but-cumulatively-expensive requests.

API-034.prerequisites: Knowledge of which third-party/upstream APIs the target application itself consumes. That knowledge can come from documentation, decompiled client code, or network-traffic observation. The tester also needs the ability to control or simulate a malicious/unexpected response from one of those upstream APIs, using a proxy or a test double where the upstream can be substituted in a test environment.
API-034.whatItIs: When the application itself acts as a client, calling out to a third-party or upstream API, it trusts whatever comes back without carefully checking it — following a redirect the upstream API sends with no restriction, unsafely loading data from the response, or displaying upstream content (like a filename or error message) without cleaning it up first. If that upstream API is ever compromised, has its own bug, or gets impersonated through a man-in-the-middle attack, the app inherits whatever bad behavior that response can trigger.
API-034.rootCause: Responses from an API the app depends on are often treated as automatically trustworthy, well-formed data — since the integration was built and tested assuming the upstream would always behave correctly — instead of being treated as untrusted input that deserves the same careful checking as data coming straight from an end user. That distinction matters because the upstream's actual behavior can change unexpectedly, whether from a bug, a compromise, or an attacker in the middle, in ways the integration was never built to defend against.
API-034.impact: An upstream API that is compromised, buggy or spoofed can push the target application into several different failures, depending on how the response is handled. It may follow an attacker-controlled redirect, reconstruct malicious data, or render unescaped content that triggers an injection flaw further downstream. The underlying issue is that the application extends its own trust boundary to cover every upstream service it consumes, whether or not that trust is deserved.
stepsToIdentify: Map every third-party/upstream API the target application consumes, via documentation, decompiled client code, or observed outbound network traffic.

For each upstream integration, review how the target application processes the response — does it validate/sanitize content, restrict redirect-following, and use safe deserialization, or does it trust the response implicitly.

Where a test double or an intercepting proxy can substitute for the real upstream response (with authorization), simulate an unexpected/malicious response (an unexpected redirect, malformed/oversized data, or content resembling an injection payload) and observe how the target application handles it.
Prioritize upstream integrations whose response data ultimately reaches a sensitive sink (rendered in a web UI, used to construct a further request, deserialized into an object) for deeper testing.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes simulating malicious/unexpected upstream-API responses against the target application's integration code, using a test double or proxy substitution.
Identify a specific upstream integration whose response data reaches a sensitive sink in the target application.
Simulate a malicious response from that upstream (an unexpected redirect location, a payload resembling an injection attempt, oversized/malformed data) via the test substitution.

Observe whether the target application's handling of that response results in the anticipated downstream impact (following the redirect to an unintended destination, executing an injection payload, or a processing error/crash).
Document the exact upstream integration, the specific unsafe-consumption pattern, and the resulting downstream impact demonstrated.

Upstream API genuinely compromised/malicious versus simply behaving unexpectedly due to its own bug — from the target application's defensive perspective, both should be handled identically via the same validation discipline.
mitigation: Treat all data received from any third-party/upstream API as untrusted input, applying the same validation, sanitization, and safe-deserialization discipline used for direct end-user input.
Restrict redirect-following behavior when consuming upstream API responses, validating any redirect target against an expected destination pattern before following it.
Use safe, schema-constrained deserialization for upstream response data, never a type-permissive native serializer trusting the upstream's response structure implicitly.
Sanitize/escape any upstream-supplied content before rendering it in a web UI or otherwise passing it to a downstream sink capable of interpreting it as code/markup.

API-035.prerequisites: An intercepting proxy (Burp Suite), access to a rate-limited API endpoint, a list of proxy/VPN egress IPs or a distributed sending capability, and awareness of common rate-limiting identification schemes (IP-based, header-based, API-key-based).
API-035.whatItIs: Even where an API enforces rate limits, those limits can often be bypassed by tricking whatever signal identifies the client. An attacker might spoof headers claiming to show the real IP address, rotate through different IPs, slightly change the capitalisation or spacing of the endpoint path, or switch between different API keys or session IDs. Any of these lets them exceed the intended request limit.
API-035.rootCause: The rate limiter identifies a client using one single, easily faked or changeable signal — like a raw IP address, or a header the client can just set themselves — instead of combining a verified, authenticated identity with real network-level details. It also doesn't standardize the request path before applying its limits, leaving room to dodge the count just by varying how the same request is written.
API-035.impact: Brute-force, credential stuffing, scraping and resource-exhaustion attacks all run at full volume against an API everyone believes is protected. The damage extends beyond this endpoint: downstream defences such as login throttling and one-time-code verification treat the rate limiter as their primary control, so when it is bypassed those protections quietly stop working too.
stepsToIdentify: Send repeated requests to a rate-limited endpoint until receiving a 429/throttling response, establishing the baseline limit and window.
Resend the same request with a spoofed `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Real-IP`, `X-Client-IP`, or `True-Client-IP` header set to a new arbitrary IP and observe whether the rate limit counter resets.
Test minor variations of the request path (trailing slash, case changes, URL-encoded characters, duplicate slashes) to see if the limiter treats them as distinct, unthrottled routes.

Rotate the API key, session token, or Authorization header value (if multiple are available, e.g. via free trial signups) to determine whether limits are tracked per-credential rather than per-client/network.

If a distributed set of egress IPs is available (multiple cloud regions or residential proxies, used only with authorization), distribute requests across them to confirm whether limiting is bypassed purely via IP rotation.
exploitationSteps: Automate a request loop that rotates the identified bypass signal (spoofed header value, path variation, or credential) on every request.
Drive the automated tool against the target endpoint at a rate well above the documented/observed limit.
Confirm and document the achieved request-per-second rate compared to the intended limit as evidence of the bypass.

Where distributed egress IPs were used, document the number of distinct source IPs required to sustain the bypass, since this informs whether IP-reputation/velocity-based detection (rather than simple rate limiting) is the more realistic mitigation.

Report the specific bypass vector confirmed (header spoofing vs. path variation vs. credential rotation vs. IP distribution) since each requires a distinct fix — validating X-Forwarded-For only from trusted proxies, canonicalizing paths before limiter evaluation, or layering IP-reputation-based throttling beneath the per-credential limit.
