examplePayloads.command: for i in $(seq 1 50); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com/api/login -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.$i" -d 'user=admin&pass=guess'; done

examplePayloads.label: Path normalization bypass attempt
examplePayloads.command: curl -s https://example.com/api/login; curl -s https://example.com/api//login; curl -s https://example.com/API/login; curl -s https://example.com/api/login/

examplePayloads.label: Credential rotation bypass loop
examplePayloads.command: for key in key1 key2 key3; do curl -s https://example.com/api/data -H "Authorization: Bearer $key"; done

variants: Rate limit bypass via HTTP/2 request multiplexing over a single connection where the limiter counts connections rather than logical requests.
Bypass via alternate API versions or gateway routes (v1 vs v2, internal vs public hostname) that enforce inconsistent or absent limits for the same underlying operation.
GraphQL batching/aliasing bypass of a per-HTTP-request limiter (see related GraphQL-specific findings).
mitigation: Enforce rate limiting based on authenticated identity (API key, user/session ID) in combination with network-layer signals, and only trust `X-Forwarded-For`-style headers from verified, configured trusted proxies.
Normalize request paths and methods before rate-limit bucket assignment so cosmetic variations cannot create separate, unthrottled buckets.
Apply a global, gateway-level rate limit in addition to per-credential limits so distributed/rotated-identity attacks are still capped.
Monitor for anomalous patterns (many distinct IPs/keys targeting the same sensitive endpoint in a short window) and apply adaptive throttling or CAPTCHA challenges.

API-339.prerequisites: A gRPC or protobuf-based service reachable from the tester's position, whether public or internal. Network access to the service port and a gRPC client capable of dynamic invocation. Where reflection is disabled, access to the .proto definitions from a repository or a client binary. Authorisation to enumerate and invoke service methods.
API-339.whatItIs: gRPC services are often treated as internal plumbing and tested less than the REST surface in front of them. Server reflection, enabled by default in many frameworks and commonly left on in production, lets any client enumerate every service, method and message type without documentation. Authorisation is then frequently applied at the gateway that fronts the service rather than per method, so a client reaching the service directly bypasses it entirely.
API-339.rootCause: Reflection exists to make development tooling work and is rarely disabled at release because nothing breaks when it stays on. Interceptors that enforce authentication are commonly registered for a subset of methods, or applied at the edge on the assumption that the service is unreachable from outside. Binary framing also gives a false sense of obscurity, so teams assume the interface is impractical to explore when tooling makes it trivial.
API-339.impact: An attacker obtains a complete map of the internal service surface, including administrative and internal-only methods that were never exposed through the public API. Where per-method authorisation is missing, those methods can be invoked directly, frequently with the service's own broad trust. Because the calls are structurally valid, they appear in logs as ordinary traffic, and gateway-level monitoring never sees them at all.
stepsToIdentify: Identify gRPC endpoints from network scanning, client binaries, or infrastructure configuration.
Attempt server reflection to enumerate services, methods and message definitions.
Where reflection is disabled, recover the .proto definitions from a repository, a client artifact, or observed traffic.
Determine whether authentication is enforced per method or only at a fronting gateway.
Test whether the service is reachable directly, bypassing the gateway, from the tester's network position.
Compare the enumerated method list against the documented public API to identify internal-only methods.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers direct invocation of the service's methods.
Enumerate the full service surface via reflection and record every method not present in the public documentation.
Invoke a read-only method without credentials and record whether it returns data or an authentication error.
Where a gateway enforces authorisation, repeat the call directly against the backend to test whether the control is bypassed.
Identify methods whose names suggest administrative or internal function and confirm their reachability without acting on them.
Report per method, since authorisation gaps in gRPC are typically inconsistent rather than uniform.

variants: gRPC-Web fronted by a proxy, where the proxy enforces authorisation and the backend does not.
A streaming method with authorisation checked only at stream establishment and not per message.
Metadata-based authentication where the token is read but its claims are never validated against the method being called.
An internal service mesh where mutual TLS authenticates the caller's workload but no authorisation decision follows.
mitigation: Disable server reflection in production builds, treating it as a development-only facility.
Enforce authentication and authorisation in a server interceptor applied to every method by default, with exemptions listed explicitly.
Authorise per method against the caller's identity rather than relying on a fronting gateway.
Re-authorise on each message of a streaming method rather than only at stream establishment.
Restrict network reachability so backend services cannot be called directly from outside the mesh.
Include the gRPC surface in API inventory and testing, since it is frequently omitted from both.

API-340.prerequisites: An application that receives webhooks from a third party: payment processors, version control systems, messaging platforms or SaaS integrations. The webhook receiver endpoint, which is typically discoverable from documentation, client-side configuration or provider settings. Authorisation to send crafted requests to the receiver.
API-340.whatItIs: A webhook receiver is an unauthenticated public endpoint whose entire security rests on verifying that the request genuinely came from the provider. Receivers commonly skip that check, verify it incorrectly, or verify it in a way that can be bypassed. Because webhooks usually drive state changes — marking a payment complete, provisioning access, triggering a deployment — forging one lets an attacker cause those state changes directly.
API-340.rootCause: Signature verification is the step most easily deferred during integration, because the webhook works without it and the tests pass. Where it is implemented, common errors are comparing signatures with a non-constant-time equality check, verifying against a re-serialised body rather than the raw bytes, trusting an algorithm field supplied in the request, or accepting requests with no signature header at all. Replay protection through a timestamp is omitted more often than not.
API-340.impact: An attacker who can forge a webhook can drive whatever business process it triggers. For a payment webhook that means marking orders paid without payment; for a provisioning webhook it means granting access; for a deployment webhook it means triggering a build. The forged request is processed as a trusted event from a trusted provider, so the resulting state change looks legitimate in every downstream system and in the audit trail.
stepsToIdentify: Identify webhook receiver endpoints from documentation, provider configuration and application routing.
Send a request with no signature header and record whether it is processed or rejected.
Send a request with an invalid signature and confirm the rejection is genuine rather than a generic error after processing.
Determine whether the signature covers the raw request body or a re-serialised form, since the latter permits modification.
Check whether a timestamp is validated, which determines whether a captured legitimate request can be replayed.
Establish whether the endpoint is rate limited, since unlimited attempts assist signature-related attacks.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers sending crafted requests to the webhook receiver and agree which events may be triggered.
Capture the structure of a legitimate webhook from provider documentation or from a test event.
Submit the same payload with the signature header removed and observe whether the state change occurs.
Submit with a malformed signature, then with a signature computed under a different algorithm the request itself declares.
Where verification is present, test replay by resending a captured legitimate request and observing whether it is processed twice.
Demonstrate impact with the least consequential event available and stop there rather than driving a financial transition.

Use a constant-time comparison and reject requests whose signature header is absent or malformed.
Never let the request declare its own algorithm; pin the algorithm server-side.
Validate a timestamp within a narrow window and reject replays using an event identifier the receiver records.
Treat webhook secrets as credentials: store them in a secret store, rotate them, and never place them in client-side code.
Make the receiver idempotent on the provider's event identifier so a duplicate event cannot repeat a state change.

API-341.prerequisites: An API protected by OAuth or OpenID Connect bearer tokens, where tokens are issued by an identity provider that may serve more than one application or API. Two client applications or scopes whose tokens can be obtained legitimately, which is often possible with a standard account. Authorisation to present one service's token to another.
API-341.whatItIs: A resource server that checks a token's signature and expiry but not its audience will accept any token the provider issued — including one minted for an entirely different application. Scope suffers the same problem: a token carrying a read scope is accepted on a write endpoint because the endpoint checks that a valid token is present rather than checking what it permits. Both are authorisation failures hiding behind successful authentication.
API-341.rootCause: Validation libraries make signature and expiry checks the default and leave audience and scope enforcement to the developer. Where several APIs share an identity provider, tokens are structurally interchangeable, so a missing audience check is invisible until someone tries it. Scope enforcement requires a per-endpoint decision that is easy to omit on an endpoint added later, so the gaps tend to be inconsistent rather than total.
API-341.impact: A token obtained legitimately for a low-value application grants access to a high-value one, which crosses a trust boundary the architecture assumed was enforced. Where scope is unchecked, a read-only integration token performs writes, so a token leaked from a low-risk context causes damage disproportionate to its intended permissions. The requests authenticate correctly, so nothing in the logs distinguishes them from legitimate traffic.
stepsToIdentify: Identify which identity provider issues tokens and whether it serves more than one API or client application.
Decode a token and record its audience, issuer, scope and any authorised-party claim.
Obtain a token legitimately for a second application or with a narrower scope.
Present the second token to the target API and record whether it is accepted.
Enumerate endpoints and test whether each enforces the scope its operation implies, particularly write and administrative endpoints.
Check whether the issuer claim is validated, since accepting tokens from any issuer is the broadest form of this failure.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers presenting tokens across applications and agree which endpoints may be exercised.
Obtain a valid token for the lower-value application through its normal authentication flow.
Call a read endpoint on the target API with that token and record acceptance or rejection.
Where accepted, establish what the token can reach, enumerating rather than exercising destructive operations.
Separately, obtain a read-scoped token and attempt a write endpoint to test scope enforcement independently of audience.
Report audience and scope as distinct findings, since they have different fixes and may not both be present.

A refresh token accepted as a bearer token on an endpoint that does not distinguish token types.
mitigation: Validate audience, issuer and token type on every request, and configure the validation library explicitly rather than accepting defaults.
Enforce the required scope per endpoint, defaulting to denial when no scope requirement is declared.
Issue tokens with an audience specific to each API rather than a shared value across the estate.
Apply the same validation at the service as at the gateway, so a direct call is not a bypass.
Reject tokens whose type does not match what the endpoint expects, including identity and refresh tokens.
Test cross-application token presentation as a standard part of API testing, since it is invisible in code review of a single service.

API-342.prerequisites: An API exposing list or search endpoints with pagination, which covers most data APIs. A valid account with legitimate access to at least some records. Authorisation to issue a high volume of requests, and agreement on a stop point since the technique retrieves data in bulk by design.
API-342.whatItIs: Each request here is individually authorised and individually unremarkable. The issue is aggregate: a caller entitled to view records one at a time can retrieve the entire set by paging through it, and where the page size parameter is unbounded they can do it in a handful of requests. Rate limiting counts requests rather than records, so a large page size is the cheapest way past it. Export endpoints present the same problem more directly.
API-342.rootCause: Pagination parameters are treated as ergonomics rather than as a control, so an upper bound is often absent or enforced only in the client. Rate limits are set per request because that is what gateways measure natively, which makes record volume invisible. Authorisation is evaluated per object, and nothing evaluates the pattern, so no component is positioned to notice that a caller has retrieved the whole dataset.
API-342.impact: The entire dataset a caller is nominally entitled to leaves the system, which is a materially different exposure from the one-record-at-a-time access the design assumed. A compromised low-privilege account or a partner integration becomes a bulk extraction channel. For personal data this converts a narrow access grant into a reportable breach, and because every request was authorised, detection depends entirely on volume monitoring that frequently is not present.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate list, search and export endpoints and record their pagination parameters.
Test whether the page size parameter is bounded server-side, and what happens at very large values.
Determine whether rate limiting counts requests or records returned.
Check whether cursor values are opaque and signed, or predictable enough to be constructed.
Establish whether any endpoint returns more fields in list form than the caller would see individually.
Assess whether bulk retrieval patterns are monitored or alerted on at all.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope, agree a volume ceiling, and agree that retrieved data will be counted rather than retained.
Establish the default page size and then test progressively larger values to find the server-side bound.
Measure how many requests are needed to retrieve the full result set at the maximum accepted page size.
Test whether pagination can be driven past the caller's intended scope by manipulating filter or cursor parameters.
Record whether any rate limit, alert or block occurred at any point during the extraction.
Report record volume and elapsed time, since those quantify the exposure better than the endpoint name.

A reporting or analytics endpoint whose aggregate output can be narrowed until it discloses individual records.
A search endpoint with a wildcard query that returns everything the caller could theoretically access.
mitigation: Enforce a server-side maximum page size and reject requests exceeding it rather than silently capping.
Rate limit on records returned as well as on requests, since request counts do not reflect data volume.
Use opaque, signed cursors that cannot be constructed or manipulated by the caller.
Return only the fields a list view needs, keeping sensitive fields to the individual record endpoint.
Monitor for bulk retrieval patterns per account and alert when a caller's record volume departs from its norm.

API-343.prerequisites: An API offering batch operations: a bulk update endpoint, a multi-object fetch, a GraphQL batched query, or a JSON-RPC batch array. Two accounts so that cross-account access can be demonstrated. Authorisation to submit batch requests containing identifiers belonging to another account.
API-343.whatItIs: Batch endpoints exist to reduce round trips, and the authorisation logic frequently does not survive the transition. A single-object endpoint checks ownership of the object in its path. The batch version receives a list and commonly checks the first element, or checks that the caller may use the batch endpoint at all, and then processes every element. So the per-object check that protects the single endpoint is silently absent on the batch one.
API-343.rootCause: Batch endpoints are usually added later as a performance optimisation, and the authorisation logic is written for the common case where every element belongs to the caller. Checking the whole list requires either a loop or a set-based query, and the loop is easy to write in a way that authorises once and then iterates. Where the batch is dispatched to an internal handler, that handler often trusts its caller because the check is assumed to have happened upstream.
API-343.impact: A caller reads or modifies objects belonging to other accounts through an endpoint that is otherwise correctly protected, which is a direct authorisation bypass with no unusual technique required. The batch form also makes it efficient: many objects per request, and frequently no rate limit sensitive to element count. Because the single-object endpoint is properly protected, a review that tests it will conclude the resource is secure.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate every endpoint accepting multiple identifiers, including batch, bulk, multi-get and GraphQL aliased queries.
Establish the correct behaviour by confirming the single-object endpoint rejects another account's identifier.
Submit a batch containing only your own identifiers to establish a working baseline.
Submit a batch mixing your own identifiers with another account's and observe which elements are processed.
Test position sensitivity by placing the foreign identifier first and then last, since first-element-only checks are common.
Determine whether partial failures are reported per element or whether the batch fails as a unit.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers cross-account access attempts and use two accounts you control.
Verify the single-object endpoint correctly denies access to the second account's object.
Submit a batch request containing only the foreign identifier and record the outcome.
Submit a mixed batch with the foreign identifier in the last position, which defeats a first-element check.
If reads succeed, test whether a batch write operation exhibits the same gap, since read and write paths often differ.
Confirm from the response content that the foreign object's data was actually returned rather than an error placeholder.

Cap batch size and rate limit on element count rather than request count.

API-344.prerequisites: An application using WebSocket or Server-Sent Event connections for real-time features: notifications, live updates, chat, dashboards or collaborative editing. A valid account and a client capable of establishing the connection directly. Authorisation to subscribe to channels and topics beyond those the account is intended to receive.
API-344.whatItIs: Real-time transports authorise differently from request-response APIs, and the difference is where the gaps appear. A connection is authenticated once at establishment and then carries many messages, so authorisation that happens only at the handshake never re-evaluates. Subscriptions are the specific problem: a client asks to subscribe to a topic, and the server frequently honours it without checking whether this client should receive that topic's events.
API-344.rootCause: The handshake is where authentication naturally fits, so per-message and per-subscription authorisation are easy to omit. Channel identifiers are often derived predictably from object identifiers, which makes guessing another tenant's channel trivial. WebSocket connections are also not subject to the same-origin policy, so origin validation must be implemented explicitly and frequently is not. Security tooling exercises these transports far less than HTTP.
API-344.impact: Subscribing to another tenant's channel produces a live feed of their events, which is a continuous disclosure rather than a single unauthorised read. Where the transport accepts commands as well as delivering events, the same gap permits actions. Because the connection authenticated legitimately, monitoring built around HTTP request authorisation sees nothing, and the long-lived connection means the exposure persists rather than appearing as a burst of requests.
stepsToIdentify: Identify real-time endpoints from client-side code, network observation or documentation.
Determine how the connection authenticates: a token in the query string, a cookie, or a message after establishment.
Establish whether the Origin header is validated at the handshake, since WebSockets are not origin-restricted by default.
Enumerate the subscription protocol and how channel or topic identifiers are formed.
Test whether subscribing to another account's channel succeeds, using a predictable identifier.
Determine whether messages sent over the connection are authorised individually or trusted after the handshake.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers direct connection and subscription attempts, using two accounts you control.
Connect as the first account and record the subscription messages the client sends normally.
Derive the second account's channel identifier from the observed naming pattern.
Subscribe to that channel from the first account's connection and record whether events arrive.
Test whether commands sent over the connection act on objects the account does not own.
Test an origin from an unrelated site at handshake to establish whether cross-site connection is possible.
